news.title: Nvidia halts chip shipments to Southeast Asia
news.text:
US chip giant Nvidia has halted sales of servers to Southeast Asian countries, including Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia, the Financial Times first reported on Thursday.

The decision is believed to have been taken to tighten US semiconductor export controls and prevent advanced AI chips from being smuggled into China.

Nvidia’s partners Dell and Supermicro, which package the semiconductor giant’s chips into servers, informed their buyers in the four Southeast Asian countries that Nvidia would not allow their orders ​to be shipped, FT reported on Thursday, citing three people familiar with the matter.

It remains unclear for how long the export halt would be in place as Nvidia works with its partners to ensure new compliance requirements are followed.

Nvidia and its partners, Dell and Supermicro, have yet to respond to The Independent’s requests for comments.

The move comes following new US rules imposed last week, which require export licenses ​for shipments of advanced chips to several Southeast Asian ​countries.

Earlier this week, the US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) formally added Megaspeed International and six affiliated entities to the US Entity List, which names foreign individuals, companies, research institutions, and government organisations that are subject to strict export control rules.

The Singapore-based AI company has been at the centre of the Nvidia scandal after reports emerged that Nvidia’s chief, Jensen Huang, had an affair with Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

BIS had launched a probe into Megaspeed over suspected smuggling of restricted AI semiconductors to China.

“Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang,” BIS said.

Mr Huang stepped down from his role earlier this month after the affair came to light, but was reinstated as the tech giant’s chief on Monday following assurances from senior US officials that he did not pose a national security risk.

Even with the export restrictions, the Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to alleged Chinese military-backed companies, the US House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed on Thursday.

Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer took to X, accusing Mr Huang of shipping extremely advanced chips to China, violating US export control law, “in what amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the Space Race”.

But the US president Donald Trump, has held that there is no evidence of Mr Huang engaging in unlawful conduct.

"Let me just say, I have clearance. And if I didn't have clearance, I wouldn't have done the deal (with Nvidia's board for Jensen Huang's return),” Mr Trump told CNBC earlier this week.
news.summary: It remains unclear for how long the export halt would be in place
news.author: Vishwam Sankaran

news.title: Women decry Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO
news.text:
News of Jensen Huang’s shocking return to Nvidia had barely landed when President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated image of the Nvidia cofounder holding up a red bra, surrounded by security personnel whisking him offstage, blood streaked across his face.

The image was based on a real photo taken in 2024 when Trump survived an assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, and implied that Huang, too, had survived a bid to take him out.

For many women, though, the image spoke insultingly to longstanding frustrations about sexism, double standards and a lack of accountability for men in power — across politics and business.

Meanwhile, many “tech bros” rushed to Huang’s defense over the past couple of weeks. Billionaire Elon Musk was among many people who signed a petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement.

Venture capitalist Jason Calacanis described Huang as a “hero” and downplayed the scandal that led to Huang’s resignation as less important than the United States winning the AI race against China.

“They’re standing up for the idea that certain men can do whatever they want,” Cleo Capital Managing Director Sarah Kunst told AFP.

Part of the problem might be “hero worship,” she said.

It also reflects the tech industry’s mythology around “founder mode” — the belief that companies thrive when founders stay hands-on rather than cede control to executives.

Huang resigned on November 12 from Nvidia, the company he cofounded and has led for more than three decades, amid allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman that US officials suspect was working for Chinese intelligence, triggering national security concerns.

Another of Huanga’s alleged lovers was a subordinate at Nvidia.

“This is a great example of why integrity matters,” Kunst said. “As soon as I heard about the honeypot element, it was clear to me that there were lapses in judgment that were really big.”

On November 17, board Chairman Harvey Jones said the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Then President Donald Trump intervened.

“I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC, referring to Huang’s reinstatement.

Trump himself was found liable in 2023 for sexual assault and defamation and ordered to pay millions as punishment.

-Dreaded “glass cliff”- 

For an industry with very few women as executives, Huang’s departure became a brief opportunity for the company’s chief financial officer to step into one of the most prominent roles in tech. Nvidia’s advanced chips are used to train and run the AI models reshaping modern life.

The board appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO on November 12 while they searched for a permanent chief.

It’s unclear if Kress wanted the job permanently, but women are often thrown into leadership positions during times of crisis and frequently blamed for any subsequent failure or replaced after things improve.

Nvidia declined to comment.

Australian National University Professor Michelle Ryan coined a term over two decades ago that describes this situation: the “glass cliff” — women or other under-represented people being appointed to senior roles during a crisis, when risk of failure is high.

Ryan is also the director of the university’s Global Institute for Women’s Leadership.

A “glass cliff” situation can also come with intense scrutiny, Ryan told AFP last week, before Huang’s reinstatement.

“When you’re dealing with a crisis, there’s a whole lot of things that you have to be dealing with. It’s not just sort of everyday business and just get on with being a CEO,” Ryan said.

Kress tried to reassure analysts and investors that it was “business as usual” during Nvidia’s quarterly earning call on November 17, when the company reported blockbuster results.

“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing, our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this,” Kress said on the call.

The results turned out to be a brief salve for Nvidia’s share price, which dropped nearly three percent the following day after already losing more than a quarter of its market value since the initial revelations concerning Huang in late October.

“I can say with a high degree of certainty that what the interim CEO will face, and is facing, is a question of legitimacy,” Berkeley Professor Laura Kray told AFP last week. Her research includes the intersection of gender and business management.

Ultimately, a multifaceted pressure campaign from employees, billionaires and President Trump ended Kress’s tenure as CEO prematurely.
news.summary:
Women criticise Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO after his resignation over alleged affairs, saying it shows double standards for powerful men in tech.

news.title: India-US trade pact and tariffs: An explainer
news.text: New Delhi, Nov 27 India and the US finalised the framework for the first phase of their bilateral trade agreement (BTA) in February this year, following negotiations that were launched in February 2025. But changes in Washington's tariff structure have brought the two sides back to the negotiating table. The US has proposed a fresh set of tariffs on 14 economies, including India. Here is an explainer to understand the developments so far. Why this trade pact? India is pursuing the agreement to safeguard the competitiveness of its exports amid high American tariffs and secure an edge over rival South and South East Asian manufacturing economies. Why these tariffs? The US is using tariffs against its trading partners such as India to address trade deficits, shield domestic industries from foreign competition and press countries to negotiate trade agreements on terms favourable to Washington. The US has alleged that trading partners like India and China impose steep import duties and restrictive regulations on American goods while enjoying low-tariff access to the US market. What is a tariff? It is a customs or import duty imposed by the importing country on goods entering its territory and paid by the importer. Tariffs increase the cost of imported goods and can make them more expensive than domestically produced products. They are used to protect domestic industries, generate government revenue and influence trade flows. Why the US market is important for India? The US has been India's largest trading partner since 2021-22. Exports grew 0.92 per cent to $87.3 billion during 2025-26, while imports increased 15.95 per cent to $52.9 billion. India's trade surplus with the US declined to $34.4 billion in 2025-26 from $40.89 billion in 2024-25. The US is India's largest export destination for sectors such as textiles, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, gems and jewellery, chemicals and electronics. Any increase in tariffs could affect the price competitiveness of Indian products and exporters' ability to retain or expand their market share. Why tariff landscape in US changing The US announced a 25 per cent duty from August 7, 2025. An additional 25 pc tariff was imposed on Indian goods as a penalty for New Delhi's continued purchase of Russian oil. After this order, the total tariff on Indian goods, barring an exemption list, rose to 50 pc. On February 2, 2026, India and the US agreed on a trade deal, under which Washington agreed to bring down the reciprocal tariff on Indian goods to 18 pc. On February 20, the US Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariff system. The Donald Trump administration subsequently turned to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the US to impose tariffs following investigations into alleged unfair trade practices. The probes into forced labour and excess manufacturing capacity are part of Washington's efforts to rebuild its tariff regime under an alternative legal provision. On July 24, the US imposed a 10 and 12.5 pc tariff on 60 countries, including India (10 pc), under Section 301, citing concerns related to 'forced labour'. What triggered the latest developments The US Trade Representative (USTR) on November 25 announced the findings of its second Sec 301 investigations into structural excess manufacturing capacity in 14 economies, including India, and proposed additional tariffs on their goods. For India, it proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent, while indicating that the rate could be adjusted to 17 per cent if the two countries reach a trade agreement. US allegations against India The USTR has alleged that India's industrial policies (such as the 'Make in India' initiative and PLI schemes), manufacturing expansion plans, labour protections, financial practices and market access barriers contribute to structural excess capacity and hurt American firms. The report has identified sectors such as steel, solar, pharmaceuticals, medical devices and information and communications technology as areas of concern. India’s response India has rejected the allegations, stating that it does not have structural excess capacity in any sector. It emphasised that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of the trade pact negotiations. It said India remains committed to working closely with the US towards the early conclusion of the India-US BTA in accordance with the Joint Statement issued on 7th February 2026. Joint statement The two countries announced that they have reached a framework for an interim agreement regarding reciprocal and mutually beneficial trade. The terms of that pact include: - India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on all US industrial goods and a wide range of food and agri products. - The US will apply a reciprocal tariff rate of 18 pc on Indian goods, subject to the successful conclusion of the interim agreement. - Both will address non-tariff barriers that affect bilateral trade. IMPORTANT: "In the event of any changes to the agreed-upon tariffs of either country, the US and India agree that the other country may modify its commitments." - India intends to purchase $500 billion of US energy products, aircraft and aircraft parts, precious metals, technology products, and coking coal over the next 5 years. Current status of talks? India has stated on multiple occasions that the deal has been finalised and will be signed once the US tariff framework is in place and India gets a comparative advantage over its competitor nations. Comparative advantage means securing lower US import tariffs and better market access than rival manufacturing countries, such as Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand, and China, so Indian exporters can price goods more competitively in the US market. Has India received this advantage The latest USTR's report has proposed a 17 per cent tariff on India if the trade pact is finalised. It gives only one per cent edge over Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand (18 per cent deal rate) and a 3 per cent edge over Vietnam and China (20 per cent deal rate). Without a pact, tariffs against India could go up to 25 pc. However, according to experts, Indian exporters could face a tariff disadvantage against goods from several other countries in the US market, as Washington's latest Section 301 investigation into structural excess capacity covers only 14 trading partners, while the probe into forced-labour-related trade practices covers 60 countries. This leaves a much larger group of economies (including Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Turkiye) potentially outside the additional tariff action, giving their exporters a relative cost advantage in the US market. Experts view While exporters are urging the government to finalise the pact at the earliest, think tank GTRI said that with the threat of up to 100 pc Graham tariffs still looming, New Delhi must reject a one-sided trade deal and defend its industrial expansion sector by sector as serving legitimate domestic, export, and future demand. What next The USTR has decided to schedule public hearings on its proposals on January 25 and has sought written comments from interested persons by January 5 as part of the final regulatory requirements before the tariffs come into effect.

news.title: Trump altered joint statement with NATO chief, urging not only Russia but also Ukraine to prevent expansion of the war
news.text:
Following a meeting in Florida on Wednesday, November 25, Donald Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte issued a joint statement. It stated that during the talks, the parties paid special attention to the war between Russia and Ukraine.

“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions capable of intentionally or unintentionally leading to an expansion of the scale of the war, as well as the importance of achieving a peaceful settlement as quickly as possible,” reads the statement published on the NATO website.

A few hours later, as noted by Politico, Trump posted the statement on the Truth Social network, altering this passage of the text.

Now it states that Ukraine, too, must avoid actions that could lead to an expansion of the war:

“We also discussed the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions capable of intentionally or unintentionally leading to an expansion of the scale of the war, as well as the importance of achieving a peaceful settlement as quickly as possible.”

According to a NATO representative who spoke with Politico, the original statement had been officially agreed upon by both sides, and the change introduced by Trump was a unilateral decision by the American president.

news.title: Inside Donald Trump's lavish Mar-a-Lago Thanksgiving—who made the guest list, who skipped it, and what's on the opulent menu
news.text:
While millions of Americans tightened their belts this Thanksgiving amid rising grocery prices, President Donald Trump celebrated the holiday at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach—surrounded by select family members, a lavish ballroom spread, and several notable absences from his inner circle. 

Trump arrived at his Florida club earlier this week for a six-day holiday stay after presiding over the annual White House turkey pardon on Tuesday, spending Thursday morning at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach before hosting his traditional Thanksgiving gathering.

Who Made the Mar-a-Lago Guest List—and Who Skipped

Although the White House has not released an official guest list, reports detailing the Palm Beach celebration reveal that the Trump family split up for the holiday this year.

First Lady Melania Trump and youngest son Barron—home on fall break from NYU—joined the president at Mar-a-Lago alongside Donald Trump Jr. and his new wife, Bettina Anderson.

White House executive assistant Natalie Harp was also photographed boarding Marine One with the president and first lady as they departed Washington for the Palm Beach holiday trip.

Two of Trump’s older children meanwhile, skipped the Florida festivities.

Ivanka Trump remained in Miami to celebrate with husband Jared Kushner’s family, while Eric Trump traveled to North Carolina with his wife, Lara Trump, and their children to spend the holiday with her relatives.

Several high-profile Trump allies also made separate plans, with FBI Director Kash Patel celebrating in Washington with his fiancée, country singer Alexis Wilkins, and Tulsi Gabbard visiting relatives in Austin and Hawaii.

What’s on the Menu—and How Much It Costs

While the average American Thanksgiving dinner for 10 rose for the first time since 2022 following a 10 percent jump in turkey prices, celebrations at Trump’s 20,000-square-foot, gold-leaf Mar-a-Lago ballroom are far removed from standard holiday budgets.

Although the White House has not disclosed a 2026 receipt for the banquet, Mar-a-Lago’s signature Thanksgiving menu typically features an extravagant multi-course spread including a raw seafood display with stone crabs, oysters on the half shell, jumbo shrimp, and clams, alongside "Mr. Trump’s Wedge Salad," deviled eggs, ahi tuna martinis, and lobster bisque.

The main course is then plated up and featured traditional roasted turkey with all the trimmings, served alongside prime rib with creamed horseradish.

And if that wasn't enough, the entire meal was rounded off with a three-layer "Trump chocolate cake," pumpkin pie, pecan pie, key lime pie, toasted coconut cake, chocolate eclairs, and hot apple crisp.

Based on typical Palm Beach catering, floral, staffing, and entertainment rates, an illustrative estimate for hosting a 300-guest Thanksgiving banquet at Mar-a-Lago sits at roughly $125,000.

Combative Holiday Message on Truth Social

Away from the dinner table, Trump also used Thanksgiving Day to post a combative holiday message on Truth Social—lashing out at political rivals, immigrants, and his own government's economic figures following Republican losses in November's midterm elections, while also defending his ongoing White House ballroom renovation project.

Later in the day, the president made his traditional Thanksgiving phone calls to U.S. service members stationed at home and abroad.
news.summary: Two of Donald Trump's children reportedly skipped his Mar-a-Lago Thanksgiving celebration - but one guest choice raised eyebrows.
news.author: Phoebe Tonks

news.title: Game over? How Friedrich Merz became Germany’s most unpopular chancellor
news.text:
Things didn’t go to plan when Friedrich Merz invited a group of children to visit him this week in the Berlin chancellery.

With cameras rolling, instead of soft questions, 11-year-old Anna asked him: “Do you not find it a shame that you are so unpopular?”

The 71-year-old chancellor braced himself, then delivered an oracle-like answer: “If you only want to be popular in politics, then you are not doing everything right.”

Popularity is unlikely to be a burden for Merz in office, where he enjoys a record approval rating of just 11 per cent. After just 18 months, the question not even his child visitors dared ask is: how did things go so wrong so quickly?

When Merz lea his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) back to power in February in 2025 it was political comeback. But it was also a personal comeback for Merz, a quarter century after his ambitions were thwarted by the later chancellor, Angela Merkel.

But the shadow of her political legacy, and dramatic shifts since she departed office in 2021, created a hefty burden for her party. Back in office with the centre-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), Merz inherited unprecedented security, energy and economic challenges. On top of that, his administration is tackling a major reform backlog while struggling to find a German economic model for the future.

Those in the chancellor’s inner circle are hopeful that, after an eventful 18 months in office and seven years of near-flat growth, the tide is turning thanks to a rising growth forecast of 1.3 per cent this year.

With that in mind, CDU social-media managers posted on Instagram images of Merz in a Grand Theft Auto aesthetic. Their political message – alongside a cartoon Merz in a high-vis vest or as a fighter jet pilot – was about promises kept, from boosting the armed forces to tighter border controls.

Despite widespread groans, the post was getting plenty of attention until a German car rental company, notorious for its satirical images, took those images of Merz and added a bulletproof vest.

It was a bitter commentary on a man who, even his inner circle acknowledge, has a rare talent for making a bad situation worse. 

The last weeks are littered with examples of Merz handiwork. Amid endless coalition rows are frequent flip-flops, most often over taxes: on alcohol, plastics, sugar. Each day brings a new twist, a temporary solution or confusing compromise.

When a recent late-night coalition meeting over energy taxes dragged on until near midnight, Merz stood up, reportedly left the room for his scarf and bag, then returned to comment: “I’m not doing this any more.”

Eventually he stayed, and a sticking plaster solution was found, but moments like this reveal, analysts say, a lack of basic political skills for organising majorities and finding compromises.

“He came to power after 20 years away from politics,” said Prof Frank Decker, political scientist at the University of Bonn, “and he lacks the skills and experience that make for good leadership.”

Merz is the first German chancellor to never hold a ministerial office and, increasingly, not even his close aides try to finesse that fact.

Take Thorsten Frei, an amenable former Merz chief-of-staff and now the CDU’s Bundestag floor leader. At an event he attended last week in Munich, political scientist Ursula Münch was shocked by his openness.

“Frei admitted openly they simply didn’t – and still don’t – have enough executive experience,” said Prof Münch, director of the Academy for Political Education in Tutzing, Bavaria. “Frei is a nice person but not very assertive. Merz simply doesn’t have the right people around him.”

[ ‘Russia wants more than Ukraine,’ Germany’s Merz warnsOpens in new window ]

That is one reason the mood towards Merz is darkening in the CDU parliamentary party. The most recent poll saw support slide to a disastrous 19 per cent, nearly 10 points down on the February 2025 election and almost 10 points behind the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). A snap election would see many CDU parliamentarians lose their jobs, compounding a mutinous mood in Bundestag meetings.

Another striking source of rancour is among those who helped secure Merz’s political comeback: CDU grandees in party heartlands like Baden-Württemberg, in Germany’s southwest. 

After years feeling lost under the centrist Merkel, they backed Merz as a conservative candidate on a dual ticket: law and order and fiscal discipline.

The latter went out the window when, after the February 2025 election win and before his May swearing-in, Merz backed the very thing he denounced on the campaign trail: an unprecedented debt-financed investment programme for infrastructure, defence and security spending.

The Merz explanation for his U-turn – that the new parliament’s opposition could block such crucial spending – convinced few in Baden-Württemberg.

They feel had that this was no one-off and that, in their eyes, the Merz coalition has developed a dangerous appetite for debt. Some 22 per cent of this week’s federal budget was financed with borrowed money. Add in additional off-balance sheet borrowing for infrastructure and defence, and that share jumps to 37 per cent.

For CDU fiscal conservatives, who view borrowing as the devil’s work, the man they backed is now a political Antichrist.

“We fought like lions – three times – for Merz to become party chairman,” said Wolfgang Reinhart, a local CDU grandee and former state parliamentary party leader in Baden-Württemberg. “Before, 75 per cent of members here backed him and 25 per cent were opposed, now it’s the other way around.”

Amid the hail of criticism, there are some who have warm words for Merz – at least some of the time – such as his steady line on European security and on Ukraine.

“Merz is bad at politics but good at foreign policy – he gets the fundamental threats this republic is exposed to,” said Thomas Kleine-Brockhoff, director of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).

But even he sees the chancellor as a master at self-inflicted “unforced errors”: announcing breakthroughs that aren’t, then chasing runaway negative headlines.

And this negative domestic narrative is starting to seep into foreign policy, he suggests, with German public support for Ukraine military assistance dwindling below 50 per cent for the first time. Kleine-Brockhoff’s theory: voters are starting to make connections between spending cuts at home and bumper security spending. For the DGAP director, this all bodes ill for Germany and Europe in the period ahead.

“Vladimir Putin is betting on a window of opportunity, between the possible election of a populist French president and the departure of Donald Trump,” he said. “The question is, given all his domestic difficulties, whether the chancellor and this country have the strategic capacity needed to manage the looming 18 months of extraordinary danger.”

The most likely scenario for now is that Merz will limp on – at least until a May state election in the powerful state of North Rhine-Westphalia. A poor CDU result there, or in four other state polls next year – could see pressure build for a change at the top.

“But Friedrich Merz cannot be toppled as chancellor, the German system doesn’t allow for that,” said Münch. “He can only be pushed to resign.”

And that is the final irony of Merz in office. As Germany’s favourite whipping boy, potential successors are not lining up. Or, to extend the GTA metaphor: if Merz’s job were a car, no one in Germany wants to steal it.
news.summary: Even a Grand Theft Auto-style makeover cannot disguise the political reality: a struggling coalition, sinking approval ratings and a resurgent far right
news.author: Derek Scally

news.title: Chinese bazaar near Xi-Trump summit venue selling banned Nvidia chips: Report
news.text: Just miles from the villa where US President Donald Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping last week for APEC Summit, some of America's most tightly restricted AI chips are being openly sold in Shenzhen's bustling electronics market, according to a Washington Post report.The revelation comes amid heightened US scrutiny of Nvidia following reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a company customer who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.The American newspaper found that vendors at the market were offering some of Nvidia's most advanced chips, including the Blackwell B300, despite US restrictions on their export to China.During a recent visit, one vendor quoted 20 million yuan, or around $3 million, for a server containing eight Blackwell B300 chips after contacting suppliers. Other traders quoted prices ranging from $3 million to $3.4 million for similar servers.The prices have risen sharply in recent weeks amid tighter US export controls. A vendor identified only by his surname, Wu, told The Washington Post that a Blackwell B300 server cost around $2 million two months ago.Nvidia does not publicly disclose prices for its high-end chips.However, an equivalent B300 server costs roughly $500,000 to $600,000 in the US, Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Washington Post.The availability of these chips in Shenzhen highlights the challenges Washington faces in enforcing restrictions aimed at preventing China from accessing advanced American technology and maintaining the US lead in artificial intelligence.Since Nvidia introduced its Blackwell series in 2024, the US has prohibited their shipment to China over national security concerns.These chips generally considered of advanced AI processors that the US restricts from being exported to major powers such as China.However, vendors told The Washington Post that restricted chips continue to reach the Chinese market through supply networks involving Hong Kong and other locations.“If I ever wanted to be a big [Chinese AI developer] and I needed a bunch of Blackwells, I would just go to Huaqiangbei and work out a deal,” Joshua Woodard, founder of Shenzhen-based supply chain consultancy Sparrows, told the newspaper.The market attracts start-ups, independent developers and foreign buyers. One vendor, Jason Cheng, said customers from Russia and Iran had been purchasing Nvidia chips from his stall for the past four or five years.“We don’t care which country a customer comes from, as long as they can pay,” Cheng said.Some traders said the products were kept in warehouses in Shenzhen and nearby Hong Kong and demanded advance deposits before allowing buyers to inspect them.Other Nvidia products, including RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000 chips, were openly displayed at the market. A vendor said these were usually sourced through Hong Kong and acknowledged their restricted status.In a statement to Washington Post, Chinese embassy spokesperson Liu Chang said, “China’s position on US chip exports to China is consistent. China opposes the US overstretching the concept of national security and abusing export control measures, which disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains.”The report also pointed to public procurement records showing that Chinese research institutes and universities continued to acquire export-restricted Nvidia chips through 2025 and 2026, including as recently as last month.Amid the scandal, Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO but returned to the position just days later.Money habits form by age 7. news.title: Mossad chief backs striking Iran without US if necessary, IDF chief favors waiting for Trump
news.text: Mossad Director Roman Gofman has expressed support for a unilateral Israeli strike against Iran if necessary, even without U.S. participation, amid growing concerns over Tehran's alleged chemical weapons program, ynet and its parent newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth have learned. According to senior officials familiar with Gofman's position in recent security discussions, the Mossad chief believes further delays could allow Iran to develop capabilities that would make the threat considerably more difficult to neutralize. His position exposes a disagreement within the security establishment over the urgency of military action against Iran and whether Israel should wait for U.S. President Donald Trump to authorize a joint operation. About a month before the Knesset elections, Trump initiated preparations for a potential attack on Iran, prompting Israel to raise its military readiness to its highest level. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir opposed going to war before the elections, while Gofman argued that Israel should seize the opportunity to act while Washington was prepared to participate. Trump ultimately abandoned the planned attack, and Israel lowered its state of alert. Earlier this month, Gofman traveled to Washington, where he presented new intelligence concerning the development of Iran's alleged chemical weapons program. During the visit, he sought to advance plans for a joint military operation, arguing that the window of opportunity to significantly damage Iranian capabilities was limited. The Trump administration has yet to decide whether to launch an attack. Israeli officials have identified the period leading up to the swearing-in of the new U.S. Congress in early January as a potential window for military action. Same intelligence, different assessments In recent security discussions, Gofman has taken a more hawkish position, arguing that Israel should consider military action even without American participation, citing concerns that Iran is secretly and rapidly developing chemical weapons capabilities. According to security sources, the Mossad and the military's intelligence directorate share the same intelligence assessments. Zamir also supports a strike against Iran but does not believe the threat is currently imminent. The military chief favors waiting for Trump's decision and conducting a joint operation with the United States, whose participation would substantially expand Israel's military capabilities. The IDF would ultimately bear responsibility for carrying out any unilateral strike, managing the ensuing campaign, defending against Iranian retaliation and providing intelligence throughout the fighting. The military's position is that Israel would act independently if an imminent existential threat emerged. “But that is not the situation right now,” a security official said. Gofman, by contrast, believes the emerging chemical weapons threat itself warrants consideration of military action rather than risking allowing the Iranian government to acquire such capabilities. The advantages of American participation Israel demonstrated its ability to strike strategic targets deep inside Iran during Operation Rising Lion, its military campaign against the Islamic Republic in June 2025. However, a unilateral Israeli operation would differ considerably from a joint campaign with the United States. Washington possesses military capabilities unavailable to Israel, particularly in striking deeply buried facilities. American participation would also provide substantially greater firepower, intelligence, aerial refueling, logistical support and ammunition reserves. U.S. naval and air forces could also help defend against Iranian retaliation, reducing the operational and defensive burden on Israel and allowing for a broader, more sustained military campaign. The advantages of American participation extend beyond the battlefield. A joint operation would provide Israel with Washington's diplomatic backing and potentially increase the likelihood of achieving lasting strategic results. Concerns Trump could seek an early end to fighting A unilateral operation, however, would give Israel greater freedom to determine the scope and duration of a military campaign without depending on political considerations in Washington or Trump's willingness to continue fighting. Israeli officials recognize that the interests of the two countries may not fully align. Trump could seek to end hostilities after achieving limited military objectives or pursue a negotiated agreement, while Israel might favor continuing the campaign to inflict more extensive damage on Iranian capabilities. Another concern is the potential for Iranian retaliation against Israel's regional partners, including countries with which it maintains both public and undisclosed relations. Washington is also weighing the broader regional consequences of renewed fighting, and the Trump administration has yet to give the green light for a joint operation. For the security establishment, the question is not necessarily whether Israel can strike Iran without American assistance, but whether it can achieve lasting strategic objectives on its own. The disagreement between Gofman and Zamir centers on how urgently Israel must act against the emerging threat and how much risk it can afford to accept while waiting for Washington.
news.summary: Roman Gofman fears further delays could allow Iran to advance its alleged chemical weapons program; Eyal Zamir shares concerns over the threat but argues it is not yet imminent and favors waiting for US president to authorize joint military campaign

news.title: Ukraine war, Melania's short-term ceasefire, Iran nukes, Greenland: Trump details Mar-a-Lago talks with NATO chief
news.text:
ANIUkraine war, Melania's short-term ceasefire, Iran nuclear threat, Greenland: Trump details Mar-a-Lago talks with NATO chief

Florida: US President Donald Trump on Thursday (local time) said his meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte focused primarily on the Russia-Ukraine war, with discussions also covering Iran's nuclear ambitions, an agreement concerning Greenland and First Lady Melania Trump's humanitarian evacuation efforts in Ukraine.Speaking to reporters during a Thanksgiving call with US military personnel, alongside First Lady Melania Trump, from his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida, Trump said the ongoing conflict in Eastern Europe dominated the agenda."We discussed Russia-Ukraine, mostly, I would say. Most of it was focused on Russia-Ukraine," Trump said.During the meeting, the two leaders also reviewed Melania Trump's recent role in brokering a short-term ceasefire in Ukraine that allowed for the evacuation of more than 800 civilians. Trump said Rutte praised the initiative after reviewing the details."We discussed a little about the job that Melania did. He came up and he saw it, he said it was amazing," Trump told reporters. "She created a short-term ceasefire, took I guess more than 800 people out. People that probably would be dead right now if she didn't do it."Live EventsYou Might Also Like:Trump uses Thanksgiving message to lash out at political foes, immigrants, federal governmentTrump noted that the evacuees included vulnerable populations on both ends of the age spectrum. "They talk about youth-there were some young, but there were some very old people, too," he said, calling the ground reality "a very sad situation."Beyond Ukraine, Trump said he and the NATO chief addressed preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear capabilities and pointed to an expanded allied posture. "We discussed Iran, and he doesn't want them to have a nuclear weapon," Trump said, adding that NATO has "got a lot of people surrounding in various areas" and is becoming "more and more involved."The US President also spoke about Greenland, referring to a newly finalised agreement concerning the strategically important territory and thanking Denmark for its cooperation."We discussed Greenland, as you know, we made that deal, which everyone said was not makeable," Trump said. "And I want to thank Denmark, the country of Denmark, they were great."You Might Also Like:India, China and others aren't taking Trump's latest tariff salvo lying downEarlier, Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin "would like to make a deal" to end the Russia-Ukraine war, asserting that his priority was to stop the ongoing loss of life while explaining his approach towards maintaining relations with the Russian leader."I could walk in and say, 'I don't like you,' and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelenskyy and Putin. You know, they have the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other, okay?" Trump said.Trump's remarks followed his meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago. According to an official joint statement shared by NATO after the talks between Trump and Rutte, the duo had an "outstanding meeting" on Wednesday."The meeting was very impactful, with the war between Russia and Ukraine and the conflict in Iran being the primary subjects, as well as all of the record-setting achievements that we have made together at the summits in The Hague and at Ankara," the joint statement affirmed.It further noted that the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war remained a key topic of discussion, during which the two leaders affirmed solidarity towards a "peaceful resolution" of the prolonged conflict."We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," it added.Trump and Rutte also discussed "the importance of continuing to expand defense spending and investment in our industrial base, both in the United States and across NATO."The developments follow the November 19 meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Their discussions covered international security, the Russia-Ukraine war and nuclear arms control. Trump described the gathering as historic, while a subsequent joint peace declaration did not announce any concrete agreement on arms reduction.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Women express frustration, concern over Nvidia boss Jensen Huang's return
news.text: News of Jensen Huang's shocking return to Nvidia had barely landed when President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated image of the Nvidia cofounder holding up a red bra, surrounded by security personnel whisking him offstage, blood streaked across his face.The image was based on a real photo taken in 2024 when Trump survived an assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, and implied that Huang, too, had survived a bid to take him out.For many women, though, the image spoke insultingly to longstanding frustrations about sexism, double standards and a lack of accountability for men in power -- across politics and business.Meanwhile, many "tech bros" rushed to Huang's defense over the past couple of weeks. Billionaire Elon Musk was among many people who signed a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement.Venture capitalist Jason Calacanis described Huang as a "hero" and downplayed the scandal that led to Huang's resignation as less important than the United States winning the AI race against China."They're standing up for the idea that certain men can do whatever they want," Cleo Capital Managing Director Sarah Kunst told AFP.Part of the problem might be "hero worship," she said.It also reflects the tech industry's mythology around "founder mode" -- the belief that companies thrive when founders stay hands-on rather than cede control to executives.Huang resigned on November 12 from Nvidia, the company he cofounded and has led for more than three decades, amid allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman that US officials suspect was working for Chinese intelligence, triggering national security concerns.Another of Huanga's alleged lovers was a subordinate at Nvidia."This is a great example of why integrity matters," Kunst said. "As soon as I heard about the honeypot element, it was clear to me that there were lapses in judgment that were really big."On November 17, board Chairman Harvey Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Then President Donald Trump intervened."I made the deal," Trump told CNBC, referring to Huang's reinstatement.Trump himself was found liable in 2023 for sexual assault and defamation and ordered to pay millions as punishment.-Dreaded "glass cliff"-For an industry with very few women as executives, Huang's departure became a brief opportunity for the company's chief financial officer to step into one of the most prominent roles in tech. Nvidia's advanced chips are used to train and run the AI models reshaping modern life.The board appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO on November 12 while they searched for a permanent chief.It's unclear if Kress wanted the job permanently, but women are often thrown into leadership positions during times of crisis and frequently blamed for any subsequent failure or replaced after things improve.Nvidia declined to comment.Australian National University Professor Michelle Ryan coined a term over two decades ago that describes this situation: the "glass cliff" -- women or other under-represented people being appointed to senior roles during a crisis, when risk of failure is high.Ryan is also the director of the university's Global Institute for Women's Leadership.A "glass cliff" situation can also come with intense scrutiny, Ryan told AFP last week, before Huang's reinstatement."When you're dealing with a crisis, there's a whole lot of things that you have to be dealing with. It's not just sort of everyday business and just get on with being a CEO," Ryan said.Kress tried to reassure analysts and investors that it was "business as usual" during Nvidia's quarterly earning call on November 17, when the company reported blockbuster results."Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing, our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this," Kress said on the call.The results turned out to be a brief salve for Nvidia's share price, which dropped nearly three percent the following day after already losing more than a quarter of its market value since the initial revelations concerning Huang in late October."I can say with a high degree of certainty that what the interim CEO will face, and is facing, is a question of legitimacy," Berkeley Professor Laura Kray told AFP last week. Her research includes the intersection of gender and business management.Ultimately, a multifaceted pressure campaign from employees, billionaires and President Trump ended Kress's tenure as CEO prematurely.

On November 17, board Chairman Harvey Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Then President Donald Trump intervened.

news.title: French politician who stood up to Bush over the invasion of Iraq is back to stop Le Pen
news.text: PARIS: Dominique de Villepin, the former conservative prime minister who rose to international prominence as the face of French opposition to the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, is back — this time seeking to stop the far right from coming to power in France.In an interview with The Associated Press, the 73-year-old longtime ally of the late President Jacques Chirac said his main reason for running in next year's election is to prevent Marine Le Pen from succeeding Emmanuel Macron.In a country riven by deep divisions and social tensions, de Villepin is championing reconciliation as a way to defeat the far right and prevent France from descending into chaos.“It’s a huge danger for our republic. It’s a huge danger for democracy,” he said in a lengthy interview at his campaign headquarters. “I think the way the far-right designates some part of the population, the way that they can pave the way for xenophobia, racism, antisemitism, justifies the huge fight that we are preparing for. I believe that if France falls into the hands of the far-right, the whole Europe will fall.”De Villepin’s popularity soared after he delivered an eloquent speech at the United Nations in 2003 opposing U.S. President George W. Bush’s planned invasion of Iraq. As foreign minister, his rejection of war embodied France’s ideal of independence.France maintained that military action in Iraq was illegal and threatened to veto a U.N. Security Council resolution authorizing the invasion. De Villepin’s firm stance failed to prevent the war and strained diplomatic ties with the United States.Today, his concerns are closer to home. .French republic is at stakeOpinion polls have for months suggested that Le Pen is the presidential front-runner and could possibly advance to the runoff on May 2 as the first-round vote leader ahead of hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon.De Villepin warned that a Le Pen presidency would bring an illiberal shift and threaten republican values. He said her plans to give French citizens priority over foreign nationals in areas including social benefits, housing and employment would require constitutional changes.“France is facing the risk of a regime change,” he said. “Even the idea of a republic would be at stake.”A veteran of France’s traditional right, de Villepin lacks the backing of a major party but believes he can defy expectations and reach the second round by rallying voters alarmed by extremist solutions.He joins a crowded field that includes judo star Teddy Riner and two former prime ministers who served under Macron. How de Villepin — or any of his rivals — can reach the presidential runoff remains a central question of the campaign as they vie to unite the center.De Villepin has been campaigning on themes that also appeal to the left, framing culture and environmental protection as national priorities. His prescription for France centers on compromise, and giving citizens a greater voice in decisions through referendums.A call for more social justice“We need to be aware that without a certain consent of the minorities, you cannot have peace in a democracy,” de Villepin said, calling for greater social justice.He argues that inherited privilege, stalled social mobility and unequal taxation undermine trust and social cohesion, leaving many voters convinced that the political system no longer serves them.“We are a society of heirs, people inheriting their position,” he said.On the international stage, de Villepin wants Europe to be more assertive, urging the bloc to push back against President Donald Trump’s tariffs and take greater diplomatic initiative on Ukraine and the Middle East.“We have to explain to Donald Trump that he’s not the king of the world,” he said.Despite his determination, it remains unclear whether de Villepin will make it onto the ballot. He must first secure endorsements from 500 elected officials, a requirement he failed to meet in his bid to contest the 2012 presidential election.“It’s tough,” he said of the search for endorsements..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Trump calls US GDP numbers ‘fake’ and demands probe: How these figures are measured
news.text:
United States President Donald Trump on Thanksgiving Day accused his Commerce Department of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections, and said he wants to launch an investigation.
The charge came a day after the government raised its estimate of third-quarter growth sharply.
Trump offered no evidence that the earlier figure was wrong on purpose. The agency's published schedule and technical notes point to an ordinary revision.
What Trump said
On Thursday, Trump posted that the "REAL Numbers on the Economy," published before the election, were "FAKE," and that a correction had been issued by the government agency that produces them.
He asked why the correct number wasn't released before the election and called for an immediate investigation. In the same post he described the episode as a "massive, and purposeful, error."
The president tied the issue to his party's electoral losses in the November 3 midterms, which gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress. Later in the day he called it "A RECORD SETTING ERROR" that had been corrected "three weeks late."
The posts were not consistent. Newsweek reported that Trump began the holiday by celebrating the new figure. At 7:38 am Eastern, his account shared a message cheering that third-quarter growth had been revised up to 4.3 per cent and declaring the economy was roaring.
Less than two hours later, he was calling the earlier 3.4 per cent estimate fake. Newsweek also noted that his 9:24 am post referred to the pre-election data as "the good numbers already released."
What the Bureau of Economic Analysis actually reported
The figures come from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), a statistical agency inside the US Commerce Department. On Wednesday, November 25, the BEA reported that real GDP increased at an annual rate of 4.3 per cent in the third quarter of 2026, after a 2.2 per cent increase in the second quarter.
The BEA said this was revised up 0.9 percentage point from the advance estimate, primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending. Economists polled by Reuters had expected a revision to a 3.5 per cent pace.
Other measures moved the same way. According to the BEA, real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, rose 5.8 per cent, revised up 0.9 percentage point.
The BEA also published a figure that was not in the first release. Real gross domestic income (GDI) rose 4.4 per cent, and the average of real GDP and real GDI also rose 4.4 per cent. That is close to the revised GDP figure, which suggests the stronger reading is not an outlier.
Not everything improved. The BEA said a decrease in exports partly offset the gains from investment, consumer spending and government spending.
How GDP is measured
GDP is the broadest scorecard for the size and speed of the US economy. The BEA defines it as the value of goods and services produced by the economy, less the value of goods and services used up in production.
The expenditures approach
The headline number is built mainly from the spending side. GDP equals the sum of personal consumption expenditures, gross private domestic investment, net exports of goods and services, and government consumption expenditures and gross investment.
In shorthand, it is consumer spending, business and housing investment, government spending, and exports minus imports.
Imports are subtracted so that GDP counts only what is produced domestically. This is why a surge in imports can weigh on growth even when Americans are spending more. The BEA's release for the third quarter noted that imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased.
The income approach
GDP has a counterpart called gross domestic income. According to the BEA, GDI is the sum of incomes earned and costs incurred in producing GDP. The two are conceptually equal, but in practice they differ because they use largely independent source data.
That makes GDI a useful cross-check. The BEA did not publish advance estimates of GDI in October.
A BEA explainer notes that the expenditures approach is the only method BEA can use for an advance estimate, since the other approaches need data that are not available in time.
Real versus nominal
The headline growth rate is "real," meaning it is adjusted for inflation. The BEA explains that current-dollar, or nominal, estimates are valued at the prices of the period, while real values exclude the effects of price changes.
The BEA uses a Fisher chain-weighted formula with a reference year, currently 2017, to calculate quantity and price indexes. In the third-quarter second estimate, nominal GDP rose at a 6.2 per cent annual rate, while real GDP rose 4.3 per cent.
Why growth is quoted at an "annual rate"
Quarterly growth is expressed as if the quarter's pace continued for a full year. The BEA states that quarterly seasonally adjusted values are expressed at annual rates, which makes them easier to compare with related and historical data.
The 4.3 per cent headline therefore corresponds to 1.1 per cent growth at a quarterly rate.
Three estimates for every quarter
The BEA publishes each quarter's GDP in stages. The "advance" estimate comes near the end of the month after the quarter ends and uses source data that are incomplete or subject to revision by the source agency.
The "second" and "third" estimates arrive about one and two months later and use more detailed, more comprehensive data.
The revision process is built into the system. Source agencies such as the Census Bureau, the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Energy Department keep delivering fuller data after the first estimate.
The BEA states that later estimates are based on more detailed and more comprehensive data as they become available. Annual updates each September and comprehensive reviews about every five years can revise numbers further.
Why the third-quarter number changed
The BEA's technical notes explain the 0.9-point revision, with each driver tied to a named data source.
 Business investment: The revision to investment was led by intellectual property products, notably software, based primarily on revisions to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Producer Price Index for system and application software publishing. A change in a price index feeds directly into real, inflation-adjusted output.
 Consumer goods: Goods spending was revised up, led by pharmaceuticals, recreational goods and vehicles, and gasoline and other energy goods, based on revised Census Bureau retail data and new Energy Department data.
 Health care services: Pulling the other way, the largest contributor to a downward revision in services was health care, based on newly available Census Bureau Quarterly Services Survey data.
 Overall consumer spending: One report put household spending growth at 4.2 per cent, up from 3.8 per cent in the advance estimate.
In short, the upgrade came from outside statistical inputs that were revised or arrived after the first estimate. The BEA's own notes do not attribute it to a correction of a mistake.
Was the revision unusually large?
A 0.9-point change is bigger than average, but it is not a record. The BEA's published figures show that the average revision from the advance to the second estimate, without regard to sign, is 0.5 percentage point, based on estimates from 1996 through 2025.
Separately, a May article co-authored by BEA Director Vipin Arora found that estimates released 90 days after the initial estimates differed by about 0.52 percentage points on average this century.
Larger revisions have happened. The first estimate for the fourth quarter of 2008 showed a 3.8 per cent annual decline, which the bureau revised a month later to a 6.2 per cent decline, a swing of 2.4 points.
A larger revision came during Trump's first term, when second-quarter 2020 GDP growth was revised up by 1.2 percentage points.
The direction of the revision also fits the BEA's own description of how early estimates work. Advance figures lack complete data on items such as inventories, trade and services spending. The agency says this can make GDP estimates differ from the final numbers.
Testing Trump's claims
Trump's specific claims can be checked against the BEA's public schedule.
The October 29 advance estimate ended with a notice giving the next release date as November 25, and the date was already on BEA's 2026 schedule, set long before the election.
The BEA's own release page for the advance estimate lists the next release as November 25, 2026 as GDP updates happen on a pre-scheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.
The administration itself treated the first number as good news. On October 29 the White House hailed the 3.4 per cent figure as the strongest pace in a year, under a headline saying GDP surged as investment hit a multi-year high.
A figure suppressed to hurt Republicans would be hard to square with the White House praising it five days before the vote.
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department oversees the BEA, celebrated the revision and credited record exports as the driver. But the BEA's report points elsewhere as exports decreased in the third quarter, and the upward revision came mainly from investment and consumer spending.
Is there a pattern in the Trump administration's handling of data
Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fails to match his claims of a historic boom, which threatens the credibility of figures that businesses, markets and consumers rely on.
In August 2025, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a weak jobs report, which showed only 73,000 jobs added in July and 258,000 fewer jobs than previously reported for May and June. He called that report "phony" and "rigged."
The president has also embraced early estimates when they suited him. In December 2025 he cheered an initial 4.3 per cent reading for the third quarter of that year as "BLOWING PAST expectations."
The BEA has drawn scrutiny from the other side of the aisle too. In an August 6 letter, Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed BEA Director Vipin Arora about June changes to the agency's inflation methods, including for computer software. The letter said economists expected those changes to lower recent core inflation readings.
Lutnick has also commented on GDP methodology before. In early 2025 he advocated removing government spending from the way GDP is calculated, saying it would give a more accurate picture. That would break from how GDP has been estimated.
What this has meant for the US consumer
Strong GDP has not translated into strong public sentiment. In the midterms, 76 per cent of voters described economic conditions as "not so good" or "poor," according to the AP Voter Poll, and about two-thirds said Trump's own policies had fuelled inflation.
Inflation is a large part of that picture. The AP pointed out that the same agency reported on Wednesday that the personal consumption expenditures price index accelerated to an annual pace of 3.8 per cent in October.
Morningstar reported that this was in line with expectations, following a 3.7 per cent increase in September. BEA data showed that the core price index, excluding food and energy, rose 3.3 per cent from a year earlier.
The quarter's own price measures were calmer. The BEA said the PCE price index rose 2.1 per cent in the third quarter and the core measure rose 2.5 per cent, both unchanged from the earlier estimate.
Strong output growth and elevated consumer price inflation can coexist, and that mix helps explain why voters and the headline GDP number can seem to be telling different stories.
The third-quarter number can still change. The BEA's release states that the next release is the third estimate on December 23, 2026, which will supersede the current data.
Because the latest revision rested largely on a software price index, the figure may move again when the third estimate arrives.

news.title: India-US trade pact and tariffs: An explainer
news.text: NEW DELHI: India and the US finalised the framework for the first phase of their bilateral trade agreement (BTA) in February this year, following negotiations that were launched in February 2025.But changes in Washington's tariff structure have brought the two sides back to the negotiating table.The US has proposed a fresh set of tariffs on 14 economies, including India. Here is an explainer to understand the developments so far.WHY THIS TRADE PACT?India is pursuing the agreement to safeguard the competitiveness of its exports amid high American tariffs and secure an edge over rival South and South East Asian manufacturing economies.WHY THESE TARIFFS?The US is using tariffs against its trading partners such as India to address trade deficits, shield domestic industries from foreign competition and press countries to negotiate trade agreements on terms favourable to Washington.The US has alleged that trading partners like India and China impose steep import duties and restrictive regulations on American goods while enjoying low-tariff access to the US market.WHAT IS A TARIFF?It is a customs or import duty imposed by the importing country on goods entering its territory and paid by the importer. Tariffs increase the cost of imported goods and can make them more expensive than domestically produced products. They are used to protect domestic industries, generate government revenue and influence trade flows..WHY US MARKET IMPORTANT FOR INDIA?The US has been India's largest trading partner since 2021-22. Exports grew 0.92 pc to USD 87.3 billion during 2025-26, while imports increased 15.95 per cent to USD 52.9 billion. India's trade surplus with the US declined to USD 34.4 billion in 2025-26 from USD 40.89 billion in 2024-25.The US is India's largest export destination for sectors such as textiles, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, gems and jewellery, chemicals and electronics.Any increase in tariffs could affect the price competitiveness of Indian products and exporters' ability to retain or expand their market share.WHY TARIFF LANDSCAPE IN US CHANGING?The US announced a 25 pc duty from August 7, 2025. An additional 25 pc tariff was imposed on Indian goods as a penalty for New Delhi's continued purchase of Russian oil. After this order, the total tariff on Indian goods, barring an exemption list, rose to 50 pc.On February 2, 2026, India and the US agreed on a trade deal, under which Washington agreed to bring down the reciprocal tariff on Indian goods to 18 pc. On February 20, the US Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariff system.The Donald Trump administration subsequently turned to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the US to impose tariffs following investigations into alleged unfair trade practices.The probes into forced labour and excess manufacturing capacity are part of Washington's efforts to rebuild its tariff regime under an alternative legal provision.On July 24, the US imposed a 10 and 12.5 pc tariff on 60 countries, including India (10 pc), under Section 301, citing concerns related to 'forced labour'..WHAT TRIGGERED THE LATEST DEVELOPMENTS?The US Trade Representative (USTR) on November 25 announced the findings of its second Sec 301 investigations into structural excess manufacturing capacity in 14 economies, including India, and proposed additional tariffs on their goods.For India, it proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent, while indicating that the rate could be adjusted to 17 per cent if the two countries reach a trade agreement.US ALLEGATIONS ON INDIA?The USTR has alleged that India's industrial policies (such as the 'Make in India' initiative and PLI schemes), manufacturing expansion plans, labour protections, financial practices and market access barriers contribute to structural excess capacity and hurt American firms.The report has identified sectors such as steel, solar, pharmaceuticals, medical devices and information and communications technology as areas of concern.INDIA'S RESPONSE?India has rejected the allegations, stating that it does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.It emphasised that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of the trade pact negotiations.It said India remains committed to working closely with the US towards the early conclusion of the India-US BTA in accordance with the Joint Statement issued on 7th February 2026..JOINT STATEMENT?The two countries announced that they have reached a framework for an interim agreement regarding reciprocal and mutually beneficial trade. The terms of that pact include:India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on all US industrial goods and a wide range of food and agri products.The US will apply a reciprocal tariff rate of 18 pc on Indian goods, subject to the successful conclusion of the interim agreement.Both will address non-tariff barriers that affect bilateral trade.IMPORTANT: "In the event of any changes to the agreed-upon tariffs of either country, the US and India agree that the other country may modify its commitments."India intends to purchase USD 500 billion of US energy products, aircraft and aircraft parts, precious metals, technology products, and coking coal over the next 5 years.CURRENT STATUS OF TALKS?India has stated on multiple occasions that the deal has been finalised and will be signed once the US tariff framework is in place and India gets a comparative advantage over its competitor nations.Comparative advantage means securing lower US import tariffs and better market access than rival manufacturing countries, such as Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand, and China, so Indian exporters can price goods more competitively in the US market..HAS INDIA RECEIVED THIS ADVANTAGE?The latest USTR's report has proposed a 17 per cent tariff on India if the trade pact is finalised. It gives only one per cent edge over Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand (18 per cent deal rate) and a 3 per cent edge over Vietnam and China (20 per cent deal rate). Without a pact, tariffs against India could go up to 25 pc.However, according to experts, Indian exporters could face a tariff disadvantage against goods from several other countries in the US market, as Washington's latest Section 301 investigation into structural excess capacity covers only 14 trading partners, while the probe into forced-labour-related trade practices covers 60 countries.This leaves a much larger group of economies (including Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Turkiye) potentially outside the additional tariff action, giving their exporters a relative cost advantage in the US market.EXPERTS VIEWWhile exporters are urging the government to finalise the pact at the earliest, think tank GTRI said that with the threat of up to 100 pc Graham tariffs still looming, New Delhi must reject a one-sided trade deal and defend its industrial expansion sector by sector as serving legitimate domestic, export, and future demand.WHAT NEXTThe USTR has decided to schedule public hearings on its proposals on January 25 and has sought written comments from interested persons by January 5 as part of the final regulatory requirements before the tariffs come into effect..25% proposed US tariffs: India rejects excess capacity charge, seeks early trade deal.US promises India trade tariff edge over rivals.US planning to hike tariffs against India, China and 14 other countries: Report.Piyush Goyal says first tranche of India-US trade pact finalised, legal drafting underway.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: How Trump's Tariffs May Benefit Canada In The Long Run
news.text: For more than six decades, the Canadian and US economies have been closely linked. Trade agreements lowered barriers and supply chains extended seamlessly across a long, undefended border. Then came Donald Trump and his global trade war, exposing for Canada just how vulnerable those ties have made it. While Trump's tariffs have fueled inflation for American consumers, they have caused significant pain for Canadians, too. And anger.But a once-unthinkable betrayal by a traditional ally may be a historic opportunity. news.title: Trump urges Putin to end military aggression across Europe
news.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that he had urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end military aggression across Europe during their talks in China last week.

Trump made the remarks in a post on his social media platform, Truth Social.

“During my talks with President Vladimir Putin in China, I spent a lot of time talking about that I would like him to cease all military aggression against areas throughout Europe,” Trump wrote.

The president did not specify which areas he was referring to.

“The hope is that a deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine,” he added.

Trump met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping last week during a trilateral summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Following the meeting, the three leaders issued a joint peace declaration.

Trump also said after the summit that Putin “would like to see an agreement” to end the war in Ukraine.

In his Thursday post, Trump referred to a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, which took place at the president’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Wednesday.

Following the meeting, the two leaders issued a joint statement calling on Russia to avoid expanding the war in Ukraine.

“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding actions that intentionally or unintentionally expand the war, as well as the importance of achieving a peaceful resolution to the war as quickly as possible,” read the statement issued by the White House.

Negotiations between Ukraine and Russia, with the U.S. acting as a mediator, have so far stalled due to major disagreements over the terms of a possible peace agreement.

European countries have expressed a desire to participate in the preliminary negotiations, which have so far involved only Ukraine, Russia and the U.S.

Rutte has previously stressed that any peace agreement must include security guarantees for Ukraine.

news.title: Zelensky urges US to pressure Russia as Patriot missile delays cost lives
news.text:
Volodymyr Zelensky has accused the United States of failing to put enough pressure on Russia during peace negotiations and said delays to deliveries of Patriot missile systems were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine’s president also criticised Donald Trump for posting a photograph of himself embracing Vladimir Putin and describing the Russian leader as “my friend”.

“Of course it’s up to the President of the United States, but… it’s strange,” Zelensky said in English.

“He’s an aggressor, and a killer…He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” he added, comparing the image to embracing Adolf Hitler during WWII.

Zelensky has handled relations with the US cautiously since a difficult meeting with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025. Trump’s two envoys have been seeking a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine, but Zelensky said they often appeared closer to Moscow’s position than Kyiv’s.

The latest talks, held in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, produced no clear breakthrough. “The more we know, the more problems”, Zelensky said, adding that negotiations were expected to resume in December.

Trump said on Thursday that, during his summit with Putin in China last week, he had urged Russia to “pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe”. He also said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was “a strong possibility”.

However, Russia’s public position appears to have returned to its original hardline demands. Zelensky said it was also unclear whether European negotiators would take part in the next discussions, despite the US envoys having announced their involvement.

He called for “real helpful allies, who can push Russia” and urged the US to use its “power and respect”.

“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor… it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.

The US says it is maintaining a neutral position while seeking a lasting agreement between the two sides.

Ukraine’s air defence shortage

Ukraine is facing increasing Russian attacks, with civilian deaths at their highest level since the full-scale invasion began five years ago. Ballistic missiles are striking power stations and bridges, while jet-powered drones are being launched daily at Kyiv and other major cities.

Ukraine responds with hundreds of drone strikes against targets in Russia. Zelensky said Ukrainian forces could now destroy about 70% of Russia’s fastest drones, with that figure improving.

But he said there was a “very, very big” shortage of interceptors for ballistic missiles and that the US was delaying Patriot deliveries.

“It’s a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It’s a pity. We have huge questions with this,” he said.

“The deficit of these missiles – that is people’s lives.”

Zelensky also confirmed that Starlink and its military version, Starshield, remained restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine. Ukrainian drone units told the BBC that interceptor drones could no longer catch Russian Shaheds, allowing them to travel further into the country.

Asked who had made the decision, Zelensky replied: “Technically SpaceX, politically – I don’t know, I really don’t know. It’s like… ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it’s the other.”

Ukraine has stepped up long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries and vessels carrying weapons or fuel. Zelensky called the warship Merkury, sunk while docked in eastern Libya this week, an “absolutely fair goal”.

Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said the attack risked extending the war into the Mediterranean. Zelensky accepted the strikes were “very dangerous”, but said Ukraine “never attack[s]” without coordinating with its partners.

He said Kyiv was preparing for a difficult winter. Russian attacks on bridges over the Dnipro appear aimed at dividing the capital, while power cuts and damage to logistics networks have forced some residents to leave and businesses to close.

“[Russia] wants us to run away, of course,” Zelensky said. “People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don’t have a country.”
