news.title: ‘Victory at hand’ in Iran war, says Trump; Tehran says building resilience top priority, though diplomacy was part of its approach
news.text: Florida, Nov 27 US President Donald Trump has said that America has "victory at hand" in its war on Iran, while indicating that Washington is allowing Tehran to reach an agreement to prevent further loss of life. Speaking during a Thanksgiving call alongside First Lady Melania Trump, with US military personnel from his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thursday (local time), Trump said that the timing of the victory would be his decision, while expressing uncertainty over whether Iran would accept the opportunity for a deal. Trump said, “We have victory at hand [in Iran]. It will happen whenever I want it to happen. We are trying to be nice. We are giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I am not sure if they are going to take advantage of that. Many people question why - are they crazy? Maybe they are.” Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi, on Thursday, in a series of messages on his official Telegram channel, in an interview with IRNA, said that Tehran's immediate focus was on strengthening the country's resilience against external pressures, while maintaining trade routes and meeting domestic requirements. “Our main focus is on the country's resilience and helping to increase resilience against the pressures that enemies apply through various means,” Araghchi said. He added that his colleagues, particularly those working in neighbouring countries, were working continuously to meet Iran's requirements and ensure that trade routes remained open.“ My colleagues, especially in neighbouring countries, are working around the clock to meet the country's needs, keep trade routes open, and take any other action that helps meet the country's needs. The goal is for the enemies to know that it is not possible to surround Iran and they cannot surround our country,” he said. Addressing the possibility of negotiations, Araghchi maintained that diplomacy remained part of Tehran's approach, but said that countering external pressure was currently a more important priority. “Negotiation is part of our work, and we have not forgotten it, and we are pursuing it; but in the current situation, there is also a more important mission, and that is to discourage the enemies from the sanctions and pressures they are imposing on our country. The path of negotiations also has its own mechanism and is pursued under the supervision of the Supreme National Security Council,” he said. The Iranian Foreign Minister further confirmed that mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan were continuing, with both countries conveying proposals and suggestions. “The Qatari and Pakistani mediators are also still active, putting forward and conveying ideas and suggestions. This is a normal process. If there are specific ideas or views that could pave the way, these are being considered,” Araghchi said. Meanwhile, in an interview with Shahrara News, reposted on his official Telegram account, Araghchi accused Israel of making statements aimed at creating an atmosphere conducive to another conflict and drawing the US nited States into a war with Iran. “In recent days, the Zionist regime has resorted to every lie to create a war atmosphere and attribute the blame to Iran. It has become quite clear that every day they make a strange statement and a big claim; claims that perhaps only naive people, who are usually found in the West itself, will believe. This is the atmosphere-building that the Zionists are doing so that they can once again bring America into the war,” he said. We are fully prepared to defend ourselves, and we know very well how to defend ourselves. We are also prepared for diplomacy, and if our demands are respected and met, we are ready to move forward on this path,” he added. The statements come amid contrasting positions from Washington and Tehran, with Trump projecting an impending US victory while offering Iran an opportunity for negotiations, and Araghchi reiterating Iran's preparedness to defend itself alongside its willingness to pursue diplomacy.

news.title: Netanyahu: "No one in the Hamas leadership will evade us"; Hamas weighs response after strikes kill 10 in Gaza

IBM is scaling back its support for foreign workers in the US, ending H-1B visa and employment-based green card sponsorship for most positions in its largest business division, IBM Consulting. The move affects a division employing more than 150,000 people and raises questions about the company's changing approach to hiring international talent.
Employees affected by the decision have reportedly been asked to consider relocating to an IBM position outside the US or leaving the company by December 31. Those who decline overseas roles will receive three months' severance, according to a document shared with managers and cited by Bloomberg.
For H-1B visa holders, the timeline is particularly tight. Accounts shared by IBM employees on workplace forum Blind suggest that some have been given just three weeks to decide whether to move abroad or exit the company. Several reportedly learnt about the development during individual meetings with their managers.
The relocation opportunities appear to be concentrated in India. On November 19, IBM's careers website listed 1,278 consulting vacancies outside the US, including 1,125 in India, compared with just 89 consulting openings in the US.
Why is IBM pausing the visa sponsorships?
IBM says its decision reflects changing business requirements rather than a sudden shift in its overall immigration strategy. The company maintains that it had relied on US high-skilled visa programmes to fill gaps in specialised talent, but its participation had been declining for several years.
The company believes it can now meet the requirements of most consulting positions without relying on foreign-worker sponsorship. That said, it has not announced a company-wide end to visa support. The restriction applies to the majority of roles within IBM Consulting.
Business performance could also be part of the wider context. IBM's consulting division has struggled to deliver meaningful growth since 2024, even as the company has been shifting its focus towards software and expanding through acquisitions such as Red Hat, HashiCorp and Confluent.
The company has not explicitly linked the sponsorship decision to its consulting business performance. However, the change comes as IBM continues to reassess its workforce requirements and the skills it needs to serve clients.
What does it mean for Indian-origin employees?
The decision could be particularly disruptive for Indian professionals working in the US on H-1B visas or waiting for employment-based green cards.
Federal records show that IBM received approval for just over 1,600 H-1B petitions in fiscal year 2026, down from more than 2,000 in FY2025 and nearly 3,000 in FY2024. These figures cover the entire company, including extensions for existing employees, rather than IBM Consulting alone.
IBM's 2025 annual report recorded a global workforce of 264,300 employees, including those working for its wholly owned subsidiaries.
For employees dependent on employer sponsorship, losing their jobs can create additional immigration complications. H-1B workers generally have a limited period to find another qualifying employer, change their immigration status or leave the US after employment ends.
The pressure is particularly significant for Indian nationals, who account for roughly three-quarters of H-1B visas issued. Employment-based green card backlogs can also leave Indian applicants waiting for decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy.
The timing adds to these concerns. The Donald Trump administration has introduced stricter measures around employment-based immigration, including a proposed $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions announced in September 2025. It has also proposed changes to the annual visa selection process that would favour higher-paying positions.
Before IBM, other companies also faced US visa restrictions
IBM's decision comes amid broader scrutiny of companies hiring foreign professionals. Last month, Microsoft, Adobe and major outsourcing firms, including Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services, reportedly faced suspensions from participating in the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) process.
PERM is an important step in employer-sponsored green card applications. The suspensions were announced by Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling, while Microsoft has publicly defended its recruitment of international talent.
Separately, the administration has increased scrutiny of H-1B hiring practices and proposed changes to make the programme more restrictive.
IBM's move is different from the reported PERM suspensions, as it is a company decision to discontinue sponsorship for most consulting positions rather than a government-imposed restriction. Nevertheless, both developments point to the growing uncertainty facing foreign professionals seeking long-term employment in the US.

news.title: “It’s like someone saying that about Hitler.” Zelenskyy commented on Trump’s words about Putin
news.text:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave an interview to BBC correspondent Sarah Rainsford, in which, among other things, he commented on recent remarks by US President Donald Trump about Vladimir Putin.

Sarah Rainsford asked Zelenskyy what he felt when he saw the photo of Putin with Trump captioned “My friend,” posted on social media by the head of the White House. In this photograph, the Russian and American presidents are shown during a recent meeting in China.

“Of course, that is the US president’s business, but… It’s strange. [Putin] is an aggressor and a killer. He brought fascism into the 21st century. He cannot be a friend. He just can’t. It’s the same as if someone had said during World War II that Hitler was a good friend,” Zelenskyy replied.

“Maybe they have a personal relationship and all that. He could say that without journalists around,” the President of Ukraine continued. “Because this is very painful for the families who have lost their daughters and sons. And they are counting on the US president. We are counting on our relationship and on our allies. We are counting on this! How can we look at a killer when the US says he is a good friend? No, he is not a friend.”

news.title: Not Far From Where Trump Met Xi, Nvidia Chips Are Still On Sale In China: Report
news.text: US President Donald Trump met his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping earlier last week in Shenzhen during the APEC summit in China. Just a few kilometres away from the state villa where they met, sellers at Huaqiangbei market, a sprawling electronics bazaar in Shenzhen, are openly selling Nvidia's most advanced Blackwell chips to Chinese buyers, despite the US ban on exports, the Washington Post has reported.During the newspaper's investigation, it was found that vendors at the Huaqiangbei market were quoting between $3 million and $3.4 million for a server carrying eight B300 chips. Brookings Institution fellow Kyle Chan told the Post that a comparable server sells for roughly $500,000 to $600,000 in the US.Traders in Huaqiangbei reportedly form part of a vast Chinese effort to secure vaunted Nvidia chips and keep up with the United States in the artificial intelligence race.In recent weeks, following reports of an alleged Chinese espionage plot targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, that effort has only grown more urgent. A sign of this was seen in Huaqiangbei, where vendors told The Post that the prices of Nvidia chips have risen drastically in the past few weeks as their supply networks are coming under strain from the fast-moving events in the US.Nvidia chips are the "decisive factor" in the AI competition between the US and China, according to Wu, a vendor who spoke to The Post on the condition that he be identified only by his last name for fear of official scrutiny."Who can get access to the best Nvidia chips matters tremendously," Wo said.The Post said it could not verify that the chips on offer in China were genuine, as they were stored in off-site warehouses.The report comes amid turmoil in Washington, which has started cracking down on export control violations earlier this month in response to the revelation that Nvidia's Huang had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a customer of the company and an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.However, the newspaper reported the Trump administration itself was divided over how strictly to enforce export controls. This infighting spilt into public view earlier this month as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for turning a blind eye to Nvidia chips slipping into China.Aside from uneven enforcement, the Commerce Department also often authorised the sale of restricted chips, including one time earlier this month, when it approved a plan to sell nearly 580,000 export-controlled Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, per the documents released last week by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.Lutnick and Nvidia now face a bipartisan reckoning in Washington, with Democratic lawmakers and Trump administration officials alike calling for deeper scrutiny into the company's business practices and the Commerce Department's handling of the scandal.
news.summary: Traders in Huaqiangbei form part of a vast Chinese effort to secure vaunted Nvidia chips and keep up with the United States in the artificial intelligence race.

news.title: Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial: What is the International Criminal Court?
news.text:
Former Philippine leader Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial on Monday for ​alleged crimes against humanity over his war on drugs, during which thousands of people were killed.

It is one of the highest-profile cases to come before the court in its more than two decades of existence, and the biggest since US president Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions that could imperil the court's ability to function. Here ⁠are a few facts about the International Criminal Court.

The court was established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression when member states are unwilling or unable to do so themselves.

It can prosecute crimes committed on the territory of its 125 member states, or by their citizens elsewhere. Member states include all 27 EU countries, other rich democracies and many developing nations, but not the US, China, Russia or India. 

The State of Palestine is a member despite not being a full member of the United Nations; Israel is not. In Duterte's case, the court says it has jurisdiction as the Philippines ⁠was a member until he withdrew partway through his term.

There have been 34 ​cases ⁠before the court, some with more than one defendant, ‌leading to 15 convictions, including 10 for the core offences of crimes against humanity and war crimes. All 10 were African militia leaders, from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mali, Sudan, Central African Republic and Uganda.

ICC judges have issued 68 arrest warrants, with 34 suspects now at large. Duterte is only the second ‌former national leader to appear before the court for crimes allegedly committed while in power, after Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was acquitted in 2019.

Four serving national leaders face ICC arrest warrants: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Russia's President Vladimir Putin, Afghanistan's Taliban leader Hibatullah Akhundzada and Myanmar military leader Min Aung Hlaing. Kenyan President William Ruto and his predecessor Uhuru Kenyatta both appeared at the court over allegations dating to before they took office; in both cases the charges were dropped.

Among former leaders who have faced arrest warrants are Sudan's Omar el-Bashir and Libya's late Muammar Gaddafi.

The United States never joined the court and the Trump administration is strongly opposed to it, casting it as a political institution and a threat to US service members.

Trump imposed sanctions on some court officials during his first term, and this year imposed sanctions on the court itself, which Washington says are intended either to force major changes or shut the court down for good. Washington has been particularly angered by the court's arrest warrant for Netanyahu and its inclusion of ‌the actions of US troops in a wider investigation ⁠into Afghanistan. ICC judges closed that part of the case two weeks ago.

At the UN General Assembly in `September, Trump called the ICC a "rogue institution" and "an evil group of people", and urged its members to resign. The sanctions, which could exclude the court from the ‌global financial system, have yet to ​fully take effect. Court officials say they have prepared to keep ‌operating with measures such as replacing software on computers ​with open-source alternatives.

The court has rejected US criticism and called the sanctions an attack on the principle of international justice.
news.summary: Former Philippine leader Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial for ​alleged crimes against humanity over his war on drugs
news.author: Anthony Deutsch

news.title: Thanksgiving storm cuts power to nearly 1 million on US East Coast; Macy's parade postponed for the first time
news.text:
A powerful storm battered much of the US East Coast on Thanksgiving Thursday, knocking out power to nearly 1 million customers at its peak and disrupting holiday travel. Wind gusts of up to 70 mph toppled trees and power lines.

More than 908,000 customers were still without electricity late Thursday, down from 961,000 earlier in the evening. Pennsylvania was hit hardest, with over 207,000 outages, followed by New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia and Missouri.

 Governor Josh Shapiro noted that Pennsylvania utilities were working to "restore power as quickly as possible in areas that have been impacted by severe weather." In Virginia, providers warned that full restoration could take several days because of "significant damage."

Air travel also suffered, with 454 flights canceled and 2,411 delayed. Major airports in the Washington and New York City areas were among the hardest hit. The disruption came as more than 80 million people were expected to travel over the holiday weekend, which US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described as "the Super Bowl of US air travel."

In New York City, officials postponed the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday, the first time the event has been rescheduled due to severe weather. Mayor Zohran Mamdani cautioned that it "will be a heavy storm," with winds that could bring down "tree limbs and power lines."

In Maryland, three people were rescued after large trees crushed their homes. Coastal flooding struck low-lying communities, and airport runways flooded in Washington.

On the Pacific coast, high tides threatened surges of up to 8 feet and forced train cancellations between San Diego and Los Angeles.

The National Weather Service expected conditions to improve across the Mid-Atlantic overnight as the storm moved into New England. Separately, US President Donald Trump approved about $100 million in federal aid to Florida following severe storms and flooding there.

news.title: Trump wants to work with Democrats on healthcare. Can they find a compromise?
news.text:
US President Donald Trump says he wants to find common ground with Democrats on healthcare. But doing so will not be easy.

“There’s a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare,” Trump told reporters last Friday during a news conference at the White House. “I’m open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want.”

Democrats, fresh off their sweeping electoral victories this month, are seeking to make healthcare a central part of their agenda for the next Congress. But the party is still building consensus around which ideas it will pursue, such as a progressive push for Medicare-for-all and more moderate proposals on adding hearing, vision and dental care to Medicare.

The Trump administration has signalled little interest – and, in some cases, opposition – to some of the main ideas Democrats are contemplating. However, an area of potential compromise could be drug and medical service prices.

Both Trump and congressional Democrats have, for years, blasted the cost of medicines, and the president has frequently touted his administration’s actions meant to lower drug pricing, including deals made with pharmaceutical companies during his second term. When discussing those deals recently with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt, Trump suggested there was room to go further, saying, “Great things can be done between the Democrats and Republicans on healthcare”.

The two parties have also been seeking to increase transparency into healthcare’s opaque pricing structures, with the Trump administration finalising a revamp last month of rules requiring health insurers to publish the prices they negotiate with doctors and hospitals.
news.summary: The Trump administration has signalled little interest – and, in some cases, opposition – to some of the main ideas Democrats are contemplating. But drug and medical service pricing is one area of potential compromise.

news.title: Trump pulled the plug on U.S. aid to Israel – but the Israeli right laid the groundwork
news.text: The bombshell President Donald Trump dropped almost in passing during a Fox News interview on midterm election day came as a surprise to many in Israel, but not to everyone. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was not caught off guard. He noted he himself had raised the possibility of ending U.S. military aid to Israel. His choice to frame the cancellation of the aid package as a transition from "aid to partnership" was neither accidental nor surprising.

news.title: 'I did a great thing': Trump defends Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback despite security concerns
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has defended his administration's role in bringing Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang back as the chipmaker's chief executive, calling the intervention 'a great thing' for the United States and the global technology industry.
Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Thursday, Trump dismissed concerns that Huang's return could pose a national security risk. He also said the Nvidia chief was looking forward to what he described as his 'second term' at the company.
"I think it's a great thing that he's going back. When I did speak to him, he is so happy to be going back. He calls it his 'second term'... He's going to do a better job the second time than even in the first, if that's possible," Trump said.
Trump also insisted that Huang did not pose a national security threat, despite ongoing investigations into the circumstances surrounding his resignation.
"I think he's absolutely fine," the US president said when asked how he could be certain that Huang was not a security risk before the Justice Department had completed its investigation.
Trump said his assessment was based on the information available to him. "Information I have, which is a lot of information," he told reporters.
The controversy surrounding Huang erupted earlier this month after reports emerged about his extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and former executive at Singapore-based technology firm Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies have been examining whether she had links to China's Ministry of State Security and whether she was involved in efforts to obtain sensitive information for Beijing.
Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and Nvidia employees. However, he has not been accused of personally engaging in espionage. China has also rejected the allegations against Alice Huang, describing them as 'groundless', Reuters reported.
The affair and concerns about possible links to Chinese intelligence triggered scrutiny of Nvidia's business dealings with Megaspeed, particularly over whether advanced AI chips had been diverted to China in violation of US export controls.
How Trump pushed for Huang's return
Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO on November 12 after the revelations triggered a corporate crisis and raised questions about the company's exposure to national security risks. Nvidia's shares fell following his departure.
The company's board initially rejected his offer to return. However, it reversed its decision on November 23 and unanimously reinstated him as president and chief executive.
Trump took credit for the reversal, saying he had personally pushed the board to bring Huang back. Vice President JD Vance also reportedly contacted board members to make the administration's case, the Associated Press reported.
"The board decided to do what we wanted them to do," Trump said after the reinstatement was announced. He also told CNBC that his intervention had been important in securing the decision.
Nvidia board chairman Harvey C. Jones said in a statement that the board believed Huang was the right person to lead the company and that his reinstatement was in the best interests of shareholders, employees, partners and customers.
Huang, meanwhile, said he was honoured to return and thanked the board, employees and industry partners for their support. "I am going to be a better CEO the second time around," he told Nvidia employees after returning to the company's headquarters.
Huang may be back at the helm, but the investigations into Nvidia are far from over.
The company's board has formed a committee to examine whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted its chief executive and is looking to appoint a new chief compliance officer, Reuters reported.
The US Justice Department is also investigating potential export-control violations involving Megaspeed. The Singapore-based firm was added to the US Commerce Department's trade blacklist on November 23.
Nvidia is facing additional scrutiny over its business practices, acquisitions and accounting. Congressional lawmakers from both parties have also questioned the circumstances surrounding Huang's reinstatement and the national security implications of the controversy.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said the administration's intervention had reinforced the need for congressional scrutiny.
"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," Schumer said in a statement, according to the Associated Press.
Huang is scheduled to appear before the Senate Banking Committee for a public hearing on December 3. He and Nvidia's general counsel are also expected to attend interviews with House committees examining the company's dealings and the national security concerns.

news.title: Trump downplays Russia, China support for Iran during talks with US troops  - Dominica Gazette –
news.text:
United States President Donald Trump has claimed Iran possesses missiles capable of reaching Europe and downplayed Russia and China’s support for Tehran while speaking to US military personnel by phone for the Thanksgiving holiday.

Taking questions from reporters at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thursday, Trump said without “peace in the Middle East”, Iran could launch nuclear attacks against Israel and other countries in the region.

“We don’t need Middle East oil. But what we do need is we need peace in the Middle East,” Trump said, as OPEC ministers are scheduled to meet on Sunday to weigh 2027 oil production targets.

The US president and First Lady Melania Trump called US service members deployed across the region to praise their role in the war on Iran, including personnel at the al-Dhafra airbase in the United Arab Emirates and the Prince Sultan airbase in Saudi Arabia.

“Each of you is playing an essential role to protect not only our country today but future generations of Americans by ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

When asked if the US would renew strikes on Iran, the president said: “If we do something, we will definitely hit Pickaxe Mountain.” Trump also told reporters he spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in recent days.

The US is still offering Iran an opening to negotiate, according to Trump, who said: “We’re trying to be nice. We’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I’m not sure if they are gonna take advantage of that.”

He downplayed the importance of intelligence-sharing by Russia and China with Iran, amid reports that the two countries helped Tehran target US bases.

“My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they’re very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information,” Trump said during the short news conference.

“We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too,” he added.

Trump’s statements come as Iran steps up attacks on US military targets across the region. On Saturday, Bahrain reported an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility while Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed it targeted US air defence radars in the country.

Kuwait said on Thursday that an Iranian drone attack on a “vital site” killed two Italian workers and injured four others. Tehran has denied involvement in the attack.

Trump told deployed service members, “You’re going to continue that deployment, and we have victory at hand,” referring to the war on Iran.

“It’s [victory] going to be whenever I want it to be, to be honest,” he added.

news.title: Costa Rica bars entry to UN rapporteur over ‘links to terrorist acts’
news.text:
SAN JOSE: Costa Rica’s government said Thursday it had denied entry to UN rapporteur Francesca Albanese, who has accused Israel of genocide, because she was the subject of an “international alert over links to terrorist acts.”

Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, arrived Thursday at the airport serving the capital San Jose to receive an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica, a public university.

Albanese “is the subject of an international alert over links to terrorist acts,” Omer Badilla, director general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, which falls under the interior ministry, said in a video posted on social media.

“I hope this clears up any doubts and makes clear the threat this woman poses to national security,” he added.

The rector’s office at the institution, the country’s most important and prestigious university, said in a statement that immigration authorities were “blocking” Albanese’s entry and asked the government to explain the decision.

The government of Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez is a close ally of US President Donald Trump and has pursued closer trade ties with Israel since she took office in May.

Last December, Albanese criticized a free trade agreement between Costa Rica and Israel and called for its ratification to be put on hold, prompting a rebuke from the government, which accused her of interfering in domestic affairs.

‘Face consequences’

The United States, Israel’s main ally, imposed sanctions on Albanese after she criticized Washington’s policy on Gaza.

“You see the face of empire the day you touch a nerve or cross its boundaries,” Albanese wrote from the airport.

The university said it was awarding the honorary doctorate, which it grants annually to a prominent figure, in recognition of her “solid academic background, experience, publications and work exposing wrongdoing.”

The Italian independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her longstanding accusations that Israel has committed genocide and other war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, welcomed Costa Rica’s decision.

“Those who exploit their UN mandate to spread vile propaganda, legitimize terrorist organizations, desecrate the memory of the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust, and relentlessly vilify the US and Israel should face consequences,” Danon wrote.

The war in Gaza — which began following a Hamas attack inside Israel on October 7, 2023 — has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which is controlled by Hamas. Many of the Palestinians killed in Gaza are women and children.

The October 7 Hamas attack killed 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures.

Albanese was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 and like other independent experts, does not speak on behalf of the United Nations.
news.summary: Costa Rica has blocked UN rapporteur Francesca Albanese from entering the country, citing an international alert regarding her alleged links to terrorist activities. Albanese had traveled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary degree from a local university.

news.title: Trump acknowledges lack of activity near Iran’s presumed nuclear site in Natanz
news.text:
WASHINGTON, November 27. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump acknowledged that the United States currently observes no meaningful activities related to Iran's presumed nuclear facility under Pickaxe Mountain, near Natanz.

"We follow them very closely. They haven't been able to do anything with their nuclear sites that we wiped out," Trump said. "We would absolutely hit Pickaxe Mountain. But we haven't seen any real activity there."

Earlier, the US leader said the US would have to deal with several sites in Iran, noting that they could include an alleged facility beneath Pickaxe Mountain.

Iran has repeatedly stressed that the US leader’s remarks regarding a suspected new nuclear facility in the Islamic Republic are baseless.
news.summary: The president said that the US "would absolutely hit Pickaxe Mountain" if any activities related to Iran's presumed nuclear facility were observed

news.title: Trump plays down reports Russia and China helped Iran target U.S. bases
news.text:
President Donald Trump played down reports that Russia and China helped Iran target U.S. military bases, answering questions Thursday at Mar-a-Lago while phoning troops for Thanksgiving.

news.title: Trump says Putin can come to G20 if he wants
news.text: PALM BEACH, Florida US President Donald Trump told ​reporters on Thursday he ⁠did not know if Russian President Vladimir Putin would attend next month’s G20 meeting in Florida, ‌but if it were up to him and he wanted ‌to come, he could. “If he wanted ‌to ⁠come, he certainly can,” Trump ⁠said, while adding some people would not like to see Putin at the December 14-15 meeting and ​that he doubted ‌Putin himself would want to attend. “If it were up to me, I’d like to have him,” Trump told reporters ‌at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm ​Beach, Florida, where he was spending the Thanksgiving holiday. The Kremlin said ⁠on Thursday that no decision had been made yet on Putin’s participation in ‌the summit. Putin said after meeting Trump last week he would consider attending the meeting after discussing it with the US president, but said he would need to take the situation in ‌Russia into account when deciding whether to travel ​to the United States. news.title: Sleeping With A Subordinate Gets CEOs Fired. Except For Jensen Huang
news.text: Across corporate America, lying to the board about a relationship with a subordinate has reliably ended the careers of powerful business leaders.Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia suggests that rule now comes with an asterisk.The temporarily exiled leader is back at the helm despite reports that he not only carried out an affair with an alleged spy, but also failed to disclose romantic relationships with at least two subordinates, including healthcare division head Kimberly Powell.READ | Who Is Kimberly Powell, Nvidia Executive Who Had Affair With CEO Jensen Huang?Over the past decade — as the #MeToo movement made the power imbalances of boss-subordinate relationships impossible to ignore — that kind of undisclosed liaison was more than enough to seal a CEO's exit. Similar revelations have cost corporate leaders their jobs at BP, AIG, McDonald's and Nestlé, unleashing boardroom turmoil and bruising share prices.Nvidia's decision to brush aside those revelations marks a stark departure from standard corporate governance — and sets a precedent that workforce experts worry will resonate both inside the chipmaker and well beyond it.For corporate America at large, it threatens to dismantle the core notion that no executive is too big to be held to the same standard as everyone else. And in a tech industry that has long alienated and mistreated women, Huang's case represents another data point that reinforces a culture of exclusion, pushing women out the door and depriving the sector of their insight and innovation.“The board is essentially saying that it's okay to have sexual relations with your employees or someone who's doing business with the company, or your customers,” said Gloria Allred, a lawyer at the center of the #MeToo movement. “It's a slap in the face.”READ | "He's Absolutely Fine": Trump Insists Jensen Huang Not Security ThreatAnd at Nvidia specifically, Huang's saga signals that ethics rules are optional at the top and risks chilling employees from speaking up when power is abused. It also prompts questions about the judgment and prudence of not only the company's leader, but also the board that allegedly represents shareholders.“A leader who is willing to violate the most basic of social tenets around relationships and loyalty will in fact also engage in other risky behavior,” said Bo Young Lee, an AI ethicist who spent five years as the chief diversity officer at Uber. “Relationships are like a canary in the coal mine to say, what else is there?”‘Central Banker'But if Huang's conduct signaled deeper corporate risk, Wall Street and Washington didn't seem to care.Investors cheered his return by bidding Nvidia shares up more than 31% on Monday after the board announced Huang's reinstatement — praising his “candor” without mentioning his treatment of employees. President Donald Trump posted a meme on social media of Huang clutching a bright red bra, holding a defiant fist in the air, modeled on the photos of the president himself after a failed assassination attempt.That reaction reflects a blunt reality: Huang isn't just running the largest US chipmaker. He has become the “central banker” of AI, said Tracy Yue Wang, a finance professor at the University of Minnesota Carlson School of Management — a role so pivotal to the industry's breakneck expansion that investors were willing to overlook almost anything to keep him in charge.Under Huang, Nvidia has propped up the sector's growth through “circular financing” deals — buying its own chips and backing billions in debt for data center buildouts — leaving investors terrified that his exit could unravel the entire AI industry.“Silicon Valley believes he is a pivotal guy,” Wang said.‘Hunting season'Yet corporate history is littered with indispensable leaders whose unchecked power ultimately cost their companies far more than their departures ever would have. In recent years, boards that shielded powerful executives over workplace misconduct — from Activision Blizzard's Bobby Kotick to Uber's Travis Kalanick — ended up presiding over employee walkouts, regulatory probes, and multibillion-dollar reputational crises before finally forcing change.For Nvidia, the most immediate fallout may be a talent problem — specifically, convincing women to stay or join in the first place.“You've created a situation where it is pretty much hunting season for women at this point in Silicon Valley and there's no downside as long as you tell people that you're having this relationship,” Lee said.READ | Jensen Huang's Nvidia Comeback Sparks Debate Over Misogyny And Impunity For Rich, PowerfulReinstating a CEO who hid relationships with subordinates sends an unmistakable signal about whose careers are protected when power dynamics collide, arriving at a moment when women in tech are already pulling back from an industry they increasingly view as hostile. The effect, according to Kabrina Chang, who teaches courses on business ethics and law at Boston University's Questrom School of Business, could be long-lasting.“When people claim, ‘Oh, it's a pipeline thing,' or ‘There just aren't as many women,' you need to look at where does that pipeline lead?” Chang said. “If it's going somewhere that's hostile, who wants to go there?”Former Meta Chief Operating Officer Sheryl Sandberg, who famously urged women to “lean in” at work in 2013, warned in December that women are now starting to “lean out” as corporate support erodes and workplace protections vanish. The warning signs are piling up: Grace Hopper, the marquee annual conference for women in tech, was canceled at the last minute this year after corporate sponsors pulled back. A September Wired survey of more than 600 women in the sector found widespread “disparagement and discouragement” across Silicon Valley.Rushed investigationOf course, employees at Nvidia — and across tech — might also see the situation as nuanced or unique.Douglas Wigdor, a New York lawyer specializing in workplace harassment and discrimination cases who has represented women accusing high-powered men, including disgraced movie producer Harvey Weinstein, of sexual assault, said there wasn't yet enough information to assess if the case could be viewed as a step back for victims of sexual harassment and gender discrimination. The onus, he said, was on the board to investigate whether the relationships with employees were unwanted or not — and Nvidia's haste had bungled an established process.“It seems to me that they just sort of rushed through things on the termination and maybe the reinstatement unless somehow they've figured it all out,” he said.READ | Chips, China, Comeback And Congress: The Eight Cs of Jensen Huang's ReturnWang cautioned other executives against treating Huang's return as a license to pursue romance in the office.“I don't know how many other CEOs can use Jensen Huang as an excuse for not being fired if they were in a similar situation,” she said.Still, even executives without Huang's leverage have managed to weather workplace scandals — while the women involved pay a steeper price. Less than 18 months after stepping down as CEO of the tech firm Astronomer after a Coldplay concert kiss cam caught him with his human resources chief, Andy Byron resurfaced this month as a fractional chief revenue officer at a database company. The woman involved in the relationship has yet to find another job — a reminder that in corporate America, second chances rarely apply equally.(This story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Jensen Huang is back at the helm despite reports that he not only carried out an affair with an alleged spy, but also failed to disclose romantic relationships with at least two subordinates.

news.title: Donald Trump Reviews Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting, Revisits 2012 Tweet
news.text:
President Donald Trump spent part of Tuesday’s Oval Office routine reviewing printed coverage of Robert Pattinson after the actor was confirmed as the latest James Bond. The review was prompted by reporters’ questions about the casting.

According to a New York Post report, Trump asked aide Natalie Harper, “Is James Bond conservative?” before the aide supplied a stack of articles. After flipping through the papers, the president remarked, “I always like people that like me,” and noted that Pattinson had previously said nice things about him.

“That’s cute. He says nice things,” Trump said.

The press packets also contained a reminder of a 2012 social‑media post Trump made when Pattinson was dating co‑star Kristen Stewart. Trump read the tweet aloud: “Robert Pattinson should not take back Kristen Stewart. She cheated on him like a dog & will do it again, just watch.” He quickly added that the comment was from a long time ago.

Pattinson, now 40, becomes the seventh actor to portray the iconic British spy, ending weeks of speculation that had included names such as Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Nicholas Hoult, Josh O’Connor, Tom Francis, Aaron Taylor‑Johnson, Harris Dickinson and Harry Styles.

The president’s brief look at the actor’s background did not include a direct answer to the reporters’ query, but his comments highlighted his interest in how the new Bond aligns politically.

news.title: Former Philippine President Duterte goes on trial at ICC over drug war crimes against humanity
news.text:
Former Philippine leader Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court on Monday for alleged crimes against humanity during a six-year anti-drug campaign in which thousands of people were killed.
Duterte, 81, faces allegations relating to 85 murders and 2 attempted murders from 2011 to 2018, including when he served as the mayor of Davao City and the early years of his presidency. The court’s prosecutors say the victims are only a sample of as many as 30,000 people killed by death squads targeting users and sellers of illegal drugs.
It is one of the highest-profile cases to come before the court in its more than two decades of existence, and the biggest since US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions that could imperil the court’s ability to function.
If convicted of any of three counts of crimes against humanity, Duterte could face life in prison.
Llore Pasco, a mother who lost her two sons, is travelling to The Hague to attend the trial that will open on her 73rd birthday. She said she had never imagined she would see Duterte in the dock.
”This is the greatest and most beautiful gift you could give me,” she said hours before boarding a plane to the Netherlands.
”My only wish is not just justice for my children, but for all those killed during the time of Rodrigo Duterte. I hope the killings stop for the next generation.”
Duterte’s supporters have called for his release. His daughter Sara Duterte, now serving as Philippine vice president, said in a statement on Wednesday that ”no foreign court or nation should ever stand above the sovereignty of our country.”
Test of embattled ICC
The proceedings will test the court’s ability to conduct a high-profile trial amid an ongoing campaign by the United States to force its closure. Washington has imposed crippling financial sanctions and called on member states to withdraw from the ICC and isolate it.
The ICC is the world’s sole permanent war crimes tribunal, set up to prosecute individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide when national jurisdictions fail to do so.
Duterte is only the second former national leader to appear before it for crimes allegedly committed while in power, after Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was acquitted in 2019.
Four serving national leaders face ICC arrest warrants: Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, Afghanistan’s Taliban leader Hibatullah Akhundzada and Myanmar military leader Min Aung Hlaing.
Duterte will be asked on Monday to enter a plea. Prosecutors will then present opening arguments. His lawyers have told judges he denies the charges.
”There was no state or organisational policy to murder,” they argued in a pre-trial brief. ”This is not a crimes against humanity case and, as such, does not belong before this court.”
Death squads
Despite his lawyers arguing that Duterte was unfit to stand trial because of cognitive decline, judges ordered him to stand trial and attend hearings. Court sessions will be shortened to accommodate his age.
During the trial, which is expected to run well into 2027, more than 500 alleged victims will be represented in court.
Prosecutors have said Duterte created, funded and armed death squads responsible for thousands of extrajudicial killings between 2011 and 2019. Philippine law enforcement agencies acknowledged 6,248 deaths.
In language his lawyers dismissed as mere rhetoric, Duterte told supporters during his 2016 election campaign: ”I will do just what I did as mayor. You drug pushers, hold-up men and do-nothings, you better go out. Because I’d kill you.”
In March 2025 Duterte was arrested and taken to The Hague, where he is being held in a detention unit for war crimes suspects within a Dutch prison.
”For those who have suffered the most egregious abuses during the war on drugs, this will be a welcome moment in their quest for justice,” said Priya Pillai, an international lawyer who runs the Asia Justice Coalition. It ”is a significant moment in Philippine history.”

 Portmore ministers oppose AI data centres without consultation, impact studies 







ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — The Portmore Ministers’ Fraternal, a Christian group based in Portmore, St Catherine, has expressed it does not support the proposal to establish artificial intelligence (AI) data centres in the city in the absence of consultation with the citizens and stakeholders of the municipality and thorough, publicly available environmental impact assessments.

The fraternal’s statement on Thursday follows the recommendation by Member of Parliament for St Catherine East Central Alando Terrelonge, that Portmore become home to AI data centres during his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in the House of Representatives on November 17.

While acknowledging the importance of technological advancement, youth empowerment, employment creation and economic development, the fraternal said proposals with potentially significant consequences for the environment, public infrastructure and community well-being must be informed by sound evidence, transparency and meaningful public participation.

“Citizens and stakeholders of Portmore have not been consulted on this proposal. The people who live, work, worship and raise families in the municipality must have a meaningful voice in decisions that could affect their quality of life and the resources upon which they depend,” the group said.

Citing international experiences with data centres, the group noted concerns about the demands data centres can place on electricity systems and water resources, alongside their implications for emissions, infrastructure costs and surrounding communities.

“The extent of these impacts depends on the scale, location, technology and operating arrangements of each development. These concerns warrant careful examination before any commitment is made to establish such facilities in Portmore,” the group added.

It is calling for:

– Thorough, independent environmental impact assessments and baseline surveys addressing water availability, energy requirements, cooling systems, noise, emissions, waste management, drainage, flood risk and the cumulative effects of any proposed facilities.

– Meaningful consultation with citizens and stakeholders, including residents’ associations, churches, community organisations, businesses, young people, environmental specialists and the municipal authorities. Consultation must occur early enough to influence decisions.

– Public disclosure of relevant project information, including proposed locations, the scale of development, water and electricity sources, environmental safeguards, anticipated employment opportunities and any costs or obligations to be borne by the public.

– Clear evidence that essential services and community well-being will be protected, with enforceable safeguards, independent monitoring and accountability arrangements.

The group maintained that these assessments and consultations must precede decisions on siting, approval and construction. It added that their findings must help determine whether data centres are appropriate for Portmore and, if so, under what conditions.

The group shared that it believes that the holistic development of Portmore must encompass economic opportunity, environmental stewardship, social well-being and the protection of present and future generations.

“Promised benefits must be carefully weighed against potential costs and risks to the community,” it said adding that The Portmore Ministers’ Fraternal stands ready to engage constructively with the political directorate, relevant public agencies, technical experts, investors, citizens and other stakeholders in shaping a responsible and inclusive development agenda for Portmore.

news.title: Zelensky questions Trump's 'strange' friendship with Putin after bizarre change to NATO statement
news.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has questioned Donald Trump's relationship with Russian leader Vladimir Putin after the US President made a bizarre change to his statement from a meeting with NATO leaders. Last week, Trump boasted that Putin was his "friend" in a remarkable exchange with the Russian president on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. Trump appeared to be in beaming as he entered a room and spotted Putin waiting for him on November 20. Pointing towards Putin, Trump said: "Who's he? He's my friend." The pair then burst into laughter. Trump continued his flattery in a post on Truth Social on Saturday, again describing his Russian counterpart as "my friend". In response, Zelensky told the BBC in an interview: "Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange." Zelenskyy continued: "He [Putin] is an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be." The Ukrainian leader's comments come after Trump sprung a surprise on NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte after the two met in Florida as part of the latest push to end the war between Ukraine and Russia . Following the Wednesday meeting, the men said they had "discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," as per a joint statement shared by both the White House and NATO. Trump subsequently took to Truth Social to change the statement to read as "Russia and Ukraine" must avoid such actions. A NATO official told Politico that the original missive was the officially agreed statement between the two sides, signalling Trump had later amended the statement unilaterally. Trump has long boasted he could quickly broker an end to war, but has so far been unsuccessful. Now, tensions appear to be heating up between Trump and Zelenskyy. Last month, Trump claimed that Russia "has been fine on Ukraine" and blamed his Ukrainian counterpart for the increasing death toll in the war. He also suggested he would be open to attending a summit on the conflict without Kyiv representatives and told reporters at the time: "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much." Zelensky has also gone as far as saying he had been "betrayed" by Trump after a key part of his country's defences against Russia went down last month. He claimed that Trump and his ally Elon Musk deliberately blocked Ukraine's access to Starlink overnight after the Ukrainian military faced slowdowns in speed and put the country at risk of Russian attacks. Earlier this month, Trump also teased a "big agreement" with Vladimir Putin after White House meeting on the war. Mr Trump met at the White House with a Russian envoy who was on the premises for an event with First Lady Melania Trump at the time. He did not meet with visiting Ukrainian officials who also were on hand.
news.summary: Donald Trump has repeatedly boasted that Vladimir Putin is his "friend". He has even gone as far as changing a joint statement with NATO to include blame on Ukraine.

news.title: Nvidia's South Asia freeze: China isn't on the list, but it's the target - explained
news.text: Nvidia instructed its manufacturing partners to halt shipments of servers containing its advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, as the United States tightens export controls to prevent Chinese companies from accessing restricted computing technology through overseas data centres.The reported suspension follows new US export rules that seek to close a loophole allowing Chinese technology companies to remotely rent computing power from facilities operating in Southeast Asia.According to a Financial Times report, manufacturing partners including Dell and Super Micro Computer have informed customers in the four countries that Nvidia would not authorise their orders for shipment. The duration of the suspension remains unclear, with the move reportedly intended as a temporary measure while Nvidia and its partners assess compliance requirements under the new regulations.The development comes as Nvidia faces increased scrutiny over its business relationships in Asia and the alleged diversion of its advanced chips to China. Two separate cases involving senior Nvidia executives, Jensen Huang and Jay Puri, have also drawn attention to the company's network of business partners and the allocation of its AI processors.Why has Nvidia stopped shipments to four Southeast Asian countriesThe immediate reason behind the reported suspension is Washington's effort to prevent Chinese companies from accessing advanced American AI chips indirectly through data centres located outside China.Direct exports of some of Nvidia's most advanced processors to China are already restricted under US export controls. However, Chinese technology companies have found alternative ways to access computing infrastructure without purchasing the chips themselves.Companies operating data centres in Southeast Asia purchase advanced Nvidia processors, install them in servers and rent out their computing capacity to customers. This arrangement allows overseas clients to access powerful AI computing infrastructure remotely, even when they are restricted from purchasing the underlying hardware directly.Chinese technology companies, including Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance, have relied on such arrangements to access computing resources in the region.Southeast Asia has consequently emerged as an important market for Nvidia, with data centre operators investing billions of dollars in infrastructure built around its processors.However, Washington believes such arrangements could undermine restrictions imposed on China's access to advanced semiconductor technology. The new rules are intended to prevent companies in countries considered high-risk from becoming indirect channels through which Chinese firms obtain restricted computing power.What do the new US export rules sayThe US Commerce Department introduced an interim final rule titled 'Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors', which came into effect on November 19.The regulations introduce additional licensing requirements for exports of advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, countries identified by Washington as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.The rules also target overseas data centres that provide significant volumes of computing power to companies headquartered in countries classified by the US as national security concerns, including China.Under the framework, data centre operators, chip exporters and other entities involved in the supply chain must conduct due diligence on customers, including checking their ownership and control structures. The objective is to establish who ultimately accesses the computing resources and whether restricted entities could benefit from them.The regulations also provide an exemption for qualifying US-headquartered companies and their subsidiaries, subject to reporting requirements.Nvidia's reported decision to pause shipments appears to be a compliance measure as the company and its manufacturing partners assess how to operate under the new licensing framework.The Financial Times report said it was unclear how long the suspension would last. Nvidia, Dell and Supermicro did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Why is China not among the four countriesChina is not included in the list of destinations affected by the reported shipment suspension because the latest restrictions are specifically aimed at countries that could serve as transit points for advanced American computing technology.Washington already has separate export-control restrictions governing the direct sale of advanced AI processors to China.The latest measures seek to address a different problem: Chinese companies accessing the same technology through data centres operating in third countries.Under this arrangement, a company in China does not necessarily need to own an Nvidia processor. It can instead rent computing capacity from an overseas operator that has purchased and installed the hardware.The new rules seek to regulate both the physical movement of advanced chips and the remote use of computing infrastructure powered by them.Although Brazil is also included in the Commerce Department's licensing framework, the reported Nvidia shipment suspension has so far covered Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.How did Megaspeed and Jensen Huang's controversy add to the scrutinyThe shipment suspension comes amid separate scrutiny of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International, an Nvidia partner that rents computing capacity through its data centres.The company has come under investigation over allegations that advanced Nvidia chips or servers containing them may have been illegally diverted to China.The controversy also brought Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang under scrutiny following reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive who was reportedly in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security (MSS).US intelligence officials have examined whether Chinese intelligence attempted to obtain information from Alice Huang during her association with the Nvidia chief. However, the available reporting has not established that she was specifically directed to collect information about Jensen Huang or that she passed information of substantial intelligence value to China. Beijing has rejected allegations of espionage.The controversy triggered questions about Huang's position at Nvidia. He subsequently resigned before the company's board reinstated him as CEO on November 23, following intervention by US President Donald Trump.Megaspeed's alleged role in the diversion of advanced chips has added to Washington's concerns about the extent to which overseas data centre operators could provide Chinese companies with access to restricted American technology.Why has Jay Puri's relationship with Cenly Chen come under scrutiny?Jay Puri, a longtime Nvidia executive who previously headed its global sales operations, has drawn attention over his relationship with Cenly Chen, former chief growth officer at US-based server maker Super Micro Computer. The couple dated for several years and married on March 7, 2026, according to The Wall Street Journal.Their relationship has come under scrutiny because Chen regularly dealt with Puri while Super Micro was seeking access to Nvidia's advanced chips for its customers. She also accompanied Super Micro CEO Charles Liang during visits to Nvidia's offices, while Puri was responsible for overseeing global sales and chip allocation.The developments have raised questions about potential conflicts of interest, particularly amid a US investigation into an alleged scheme to divert Nvidia-powered servers to China. On March 19, the Justice Department charged Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, a sales manager and a third-party broker with conspiring to smuggle more than $500 million worth of servers containing Nvidia chips into China. Prosecutors alleged that at least $510 million worth of equipment was diverted through a Southeast Asian company.Neither Puri nor Chen was named in the indictment. Super Micro was also not named as a defendant and has maintained that it was a victim of the alleged scheme. Chen denied that her relationship with Puri influenced her professional decisions, saying, “I never had to rely on personal relationships for professional gain.” She also denied involvement in chip procurement, while Super Micro said chip allocation was handled through a multi-department process.Money habits form by age 7. news.title: Zelenskyy warns of major Russian attack as Trump urges Putin to ‘pull back’  - Trinidad Tribune – Latest
news.text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass strike on the country in the coming days.

“Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass strike being prepared by the Russians,” he said in his nightly video address on Thursday. “In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats.”

It was the second such warning from Zelenskyy this week. He also had a message for Moscow: “We will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike.”

Trump urges Putin to pull back

US President Donald Trump said he had pressed Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease Russia’s military actions in Europe.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he spent “a lot of time” in talks with Putin in China on the issue of Putin pulling back “all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe”.

“Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH,” Trump wrote. He said he hoped that would allow a deal between Russia and Ukraine to be “made quickly”, which he called “a strong possibility”.

Trump said he updated NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on the talks during a meeting at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Wednesday night.

Latest attacks

Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, wounding seven people and hitting a shopping centre and two other buildings, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Moscow said it hit drone-related sites in the city. Russian forces have attacked Kyiv and other cities almost continuously since September.

Ukraine said its drones hit an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, oil reservoirs at a Transneft facility in Bashkortostan and the Marinovka military airfield in the Volgograd region.

Ukraine has also widened its attacks at sea. On Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine used seven naval drones to hit the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo ship Angara off Libya. Libyan officials told the Associated Press news agency that the Merkury was heavily damaged but not sunk.

At about the same time, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound cargo ship Sparta II in the Baltic Sea, near Finland. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the attacks a “very dangerous trend“.

At least four Russian vessels have been targeted this month.

Europe’s funding for Ukraine

European Union leaders are struggling at a summit in Brussels to agree on a new 45 billion euro ($49bn) loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year. It would come on top of a 90 billion euro ($99bn) loan, agreed nearly a year ago, that covers most of Ukraine’s government needs for 2026 and 2027.

Early on Friday in Brussels, European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 member states supported the new loan, as talks on the bloc’s next seven-year budget stretched on.

The loan is tangled up with the EU’s budget for 2028 to 2034, which includes about $110bn for Ukraine over seven years. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to hold up the budget unless all member states make a “collective commitment” to Ukraine.

North Korea ‘pauses’ arms deliveries

Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (GUR) said on Thursday that North Korea has temporarily halted some military cooperation with Russia after diplomatic tensions between the allies.

It said this includes deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and artillery shells, and Russian military flights over North Korean territory.

GUR said North Korea’s Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui announced the pause last month in response to a Russian deputy foreign minister’s assertion that Moscow would help ease tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.

GUR also said Pyongyang is holding off on a Russian request to raise North Korea’s military presence in Russia from about 8,500 to 50,000 troops.

It added that North Korean units remain in Russia’s Kursk region and that a North Korean missile unit has been in the Voronezh region since mid-summer, from where Russia strikes Ukraine.

South Korean and Western intelligence agencies have said Pyongyang sent more than 10,000 soldiers to Russia’s Kursk region in 2024, along with artillery shells, missiles and long-range rocket systems.

Strikes continue

On November 20, Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine, killing eight people, Zelenskyy said.

It was one of the largest attacks of the war and followed Putin’s vow to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea.
